`// luxe:allow-secret`, `gitleaks:allow`, `pragma: allowlist secret` or `nosec`.

To leave project bookkeeping out of every review:

```json title=".luxe/config.json"
{ "review": { "exclude": ["PROGRESS.md", "docs/design/**"] } }
```

The patterns take `*`, `**`, `?` and a trailing `/`, and a project's list replaces your own.
Excluded files are counted in the guide. Luxe's own `.luxe/` is never reviewed.

A review leaves out a file it cannot hold, so the rest is still reviewable: in the last turn, any
file over 1 MiB, unreadable, or not a regular file; in uncommitted changes or a base, a new file
that is not ignored and is over 1 MiB or not a regular file. The top of the guide names each one,
so a review that shows less than the change never passes for all of it.

## Comment and ask

| Key | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `c` | **Comment** on the line under the cursor. It waits for you to send it: to the agent, or to GitHub with your review of a pull request. |
| `a` | **Ask the agent** about the line. It answers right away and changes nothing. |
| `alt+c` | **Feedback**: every comment, with the one under the cursor in full |
| `alt+u` | **Send** the unsent comments to the agent, from a preview where `space` leaves one out |

In **Feedback**, `enter` goes to a comment, `c` replies, `e` edits, `x` deletes one not yet sent,
`r` marks it verified, resolved or reopened, `d` shows its details, `alt+r` moves a stale one to
where its line went, `v` shows what changed at its line, and `u` sends. On an answered question, `c` turns it
into a comment, so the question, the answer and your direction reach the agent together.

You can keep commenting while the agent works on what you sent. When the agent's fix is in, the
review says `The fix is in · ctrl+r refresh`. `ctrl+r`, or `/diff refresh`, reads the code again
so you can verify it, at any time.

The agent ends a fix by reporting on each comment: fixed, not fixed, or needs clarification, with a
note. The note shows under the comment, and a comment it calls fixed waits for you to verify it,
since a claim is not proof. If the agent leaves its report out, Luxe asks for it once. A comment
the agent still says nothing about reads `no word from the agent`, with the reason in Feedback,
and stays where you left it.

## Finish

`alt+enter` finishes the review:

![Finishing a review](images/review-finish.svg)

| Choice | Does |
| --- | --- |
| **Accept** | Mark it reviewed. The agent is not told. |
| **Accept and commit** | Accept, then commit each chapter as its own commit, with the chapter's explanation as the message. Never pushes. |
| **Request fixes** | Send your comments for the agent to address |
| **Comment only** | Send your comments without asking for edits |
| **Keep reviewing** | Close this and carry on. Nothing is sent. |
| **Open pull request** | Commit, push and open a pull request drafted from the review. Offered when the branch has none. See [Git and GitHub](github.md#open-a-pull-request). |
| **Open as a stack** | One pull request per chapter. Offered with two chapters or more. |
| **Answer on GitHub** | On your own pull request: reply to and resolve the threads you fixed |

**Accept and commit** shows the commits first; `s` there makes them one. A review of a base or a
commit can only be committed that way. It refuses if files are already staged or the code changed
after the review was captured.

## Review a pull request

`/diff pr 142` reads a pull request into the same review: a teammate's, a bot's, or one another
agent opened. It needs the GitHub CLI, `gh`, signed in.

![Reviewing a bot's pull request, with its GitHub discussion](images/review-pull-request.svg)

- It is pinned to the commit GitHub reported and compared from where it branched, as GitHub's
  **Files changed** does. Nothing in your checkout moves.
- The head says who opened it and where it stands: `by dependabot (bot) · 1 failing · changes requested`.
- The author's description follows the guide, under its own heading.
- Review threads appear under the lines they are about. Anything without a line is under
  **Discussion on GitHub**.
- `a` asks the agent about a line, at the pull request's commit.
- `ctrl+r` reads it again after a new push.

### Post your review

`alt+enter` on a pull request shows exactly what will be posted before anything is:

| Key | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `tab` / `shift+tab` | Choose **Comment**, **Approve** or **Request changes** |
| `c` | Write the summary. **Request changes** needs one. |
| `d` | Have the agent draft the summary from this review |
| `e` | Edit the summary |
| `enter` | Post it |

Line comments are listed under their files with the diff they sit on, the way GitHub shows them.
Questions you asked the agent stay in Luxe and are never posted. On your own pull request, GitHub
only takes a comment, so that is all Luxe offers.

A drafted summary opens in the preview for you to read and edit. Anything the agent says beside it,
such as a part of the change it did not read, appears under it as a note. Once the review is
posted, the guide's foot says **Posted to GitHub** with the verdict, and `o` opens it.

### Fix it yourself

To change someone else's pull request rather than comment on it, press `alt+u` (or `w` in the post
preview). Luxe asks GitHub whether you can push to it, then checks it out in a worktree of its own
and starts a session there, with your comments as the agent's first task. A plain `git push` then
updates the pull request.
@@@ page: hooks
---
title: "Hooks"
summary: "Run your own commands at points in a turn: block, rewrite or audit tool calls, and add context."
order: 5
group: "Extend"
---

A hook runs a command of yours at a point in a turn, such as before each tool call. It receives
the event as JSON on stdin and can answer with a decision as JSON on stdout. Any executable works:
a shell script, Python, a compiled program.

## Add a hook

Hooks go in `~/.config/luxe/hooks.json`. This one asks before any recursive delete and refuses a
wipe of `/` or your home folder:

```json title="~/.config/luxe/hooks.json"
{
  "BeforeToolUse": [
    {
      "matcher": { "bash": "rm *" },
      "command": ["/home/you/.config/luxe/hooks/guard.sh"],
      "on_timeout": "deny"
    }
  ]
}
```

```bash title="~/.config/luxe/hooks/guard.sh"
#!/usr/bin/env bash
cmd=$(jq -r '.ToolUse.args.command // empty')
case "$cmd" in
  *"rm -rf /"*|*"rm -rf ~"*) echo '{"decision":"deny","reason":"refusing a root or home wipe"}' ;;
  *)                         echo '{"decision":"ask","reason":"recursive delete"}' ;;
esac
```

A project's `.luxe/hooks.json` runs only when you start Luxe with `--trust-project`, since opening a
repository should never run its commands. When both are loaded, a project's hooks run after yours.

### Hook settings

| Key | Default | Does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `command` | | The program and its arguments, run without a shell. Use `["sh", "-c", "…"]` for shell features. |
| `matcher` | every call | Which tool calls it runs for; see [Matchers](#matchers) |
| `timeout_ms` | `5000` | One deadline for sending the event, reading output and waiting for exit. On timeout, it and everything it started are stopped. |
| `on_timeout` | `allow` | What happens if the hook times out, fails to start, exits non-zero or prints something that is not a decision: `allow`, `deny` or `ask` |

`on_timeout: "deny"` makes a guard fail closed. `"ask"` puts the question to you instead, at
`BeforeToolUse`; at other points it acts as `allow`. A
`decision` Luxe does not recognize, a typo or different casing included, gets the same treatment,
with a warning in the log, and its `args` and `context` are dropped.

## Matchers

A `BeforeToolUse` hook without a matcher runs on every tool call, and each run starts a process.
A matcher skips the calls you do not care about, without starting anything:

```text
"matcher": "bash"                                   a tool name, or a pattern like "web_*"
"matcher": { "bash": "rm *", "edit": "src/**" }     a tool and what the call is about
```

The second form matches if any entry does. The patterns are the same as in
[`permissions.json`](security.md): `"rm *"` finds the `rm` in `cd /tmp && rm -rf x`, and a
pattern for `read` or `edit` matches the path, for `web_fetch` the address.

Only `BeforeToolUse` sees a call's arguments. At `AfterToolUse` only the tool name is matched, and
points without a tool call ignore the matcher.

## Hook points

| Point | Runs | stdin | Can |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `SessionStart` | A session starts or resumes, including a switch to it from another session | `{"Other": null}` | |
| `SessionEnd` | A session ends, including a switch to another session; Luxe waits for the hook | `{"Other": null}` | |
| `UserPromptSubmit` | You send a message, including one sent while the agent works | `{"Other": {"content": "…"}}` | block it, add context |
| `BeforeAgentStart` | A turn is about to start | `{"Other": null}` | |
| `AgentStart` | Luxe is about to call the model | `{"Other": null}` | |
| `BeforeToolUse` | Before each tool call | `{"ToolUse": {"tool_name": "bash", "args": {…}}}` | block it, ask you, rewrite it |
| `AfterToolUse` | After each tool call | `{"ToolResult": {"tool_name": "bash", "result": "…", "is_error": false}}` | add context to the result |
| `FileChanged` | `write`, `edit`, an applied rename or code action, or an `ast_grep` rewrite changed a file | `{"FileChanged": {"path": "/abs/file", "operation": "edit"}}` | |
| `BeforeCompact`, `AfterCompact` | Around compaction | `{"Other": {"tokens_before": 12345}}` | |
| `AgentEnd` | A turn finished | `{"Other": {"effective_context_percent": 12.5}}` | |
| `Error` | A turn failed | `{"Other": {"message": "…"}}` | |
| `PermissionRequested`, `PermissionResolved` | An approval prompt opens or is answered | `{"Other": {"tool": "bash", "phase": "requested", …}}` | |
| `ReviewGate`, `LoopControl` | `luxe loop` only | | |

A hook at a point with nothing under **Can** still runs, for logging or notifications, but its
answer is ignored. Point names are matched loosely (`before_tool_use` works). An unknown name skips
that hook alone, with a warning naming the nearest real point.

## Answer with a decision

```json
{ "decision": "deny", "reason": "rm -rf is blocked by policy" }
```

| Field | Where | Does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `decision` | Required in any answer | `deny` blocks the call or message. `ask` raises a permission prompt, at `BeforeToolUse`. `allow`, or no output at all, means no opinion. An answer without `decision` counts as one Luxe cannot read. |
| `reason` | with `deny` or `ask` | Shown to the model when a call is blocked, to you when a message is blocked, and on the prompt |
| `args` | `BeforeToolUse` | New values for the call's arguments. Keys you leave out keep their values. |
| `context` | `AfterToolUse`, `UserPromptSubmit` | Text added to the tool result, or saved with your message, for the model to see |

```json
{ "decision": "allow", "args": { "command": "bun test" } }
```

When several hooks answer the same point, their context and rewrites are combined in order. A
`deny` ends it: hooks after it do not run.

### What a hook cannot do

- **Approve a call.** `allow` means no opinion; a hook can only make a call harder. To auto-approve,
  write a rule in [`permissions.json`](security.md).
- **Rewrite its way past the rules.** A rewritten call is checked by the permission rules as
  rewritten, and that is what runs. If a rewritten call matches an `ask` rule, you are asked about
  the new command.

### When nobody is there to answer

In a headless or loop run, a hook's `ask` is allowed, like every other `ask`. To change that:

- `--on-ask deny`, or `"agent": { "on_ask": "deny" }` in `config.json`, refuses every `ask` in an
  unattended run, and tells the model why.
- `{ "permission": { "hook_ask": "deny" } }` in `permissions.json` turns every hook's `ask` into a
  block everywhere, even when you are there. `"allow"` silences them instead.

A hook's prompt offers **Allow once** and **Reject**, since a hook decides each call afresh.

## What a hook sees

The event a hook receives is not redacted: it is a program you installed, with the same access you
have, and the call's arguments have already gone to your model provider. What a hook returns, its
`reason` and `context`, is scrubbed of anything that looks like a secret before it is shown or
saved. Read a hook script before installing it, as you would anything on your `PATH`.

## Examples

**Add lint output to every edit:**

```json title="~/.config/luxe/hooks.json"
{
  "AfterToolUse": [
    {
      "matcher": "edit",
      "command": ["sh", "-c", "jq -n --arg out \"$(npm run -s lint 2>&1 | tail -20)\" '{decision: \"allow\", context: $out}'"]
    }
  ]
}
```

Luxe already adds language server errors after every edit; a hook like this is for a different
check.

**Refuse messages that contain an internal token:**

```bash title="~/.config/luxe/hooks/prompt-policy.sh"
#!/usr/bin/env bash
prompt=$(jq -r '.Other.content // empty')
if printf '%s' "$prompt" | grep -qE 'CORP-SECRET-[0-9]+'; then
  echo '{"decision":"deny","reason":"the message contained an internal token"}'
fi
```

**Copy the sessions before compaction:**

```json title="~/.config/luxe/hooks.json"
{ "BeforeCompact": [{ "command": ["sh", "-c", "cp -r .luxe/sessions /tmp/luxe-precompact-$$"] }] }
```

[Recipes](recipes.md#a-guard-that-asks-a-model) has a hook that asks a classifier model whether a
command is destructive.

## Coming from Claude Code

| Claude Code | Luxe |
| --- | --- |
| `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse` | `BeforeToolUse`, `AfterToolUse` |
| `UserPromptSubmit` with `additionalContext` | `UserPromptSubmit` with `context` |
| `SessionStart`, `SessionEnd` | the same |
| `PreCompact`, `PostCompact` | `BeforeCompact`, `AfterCompact` |
| `Stop` | `AgentEnd`, which observes only |
| `permissionDecision: "ask"` | `"decision": "ask"` |
| `updatedInput` | `args`, checked again by the permission rules |
| `matcher` and `if` | `matcher`, in either form |
| `permissionDecision: "allow"`, which skips the prompt | No equivalent: use `permissions.json` |
@@@ page: index
---
title: "Overview"
summary: "What Luxe is, and where to find what you need."
order: 0
group: "Get started"
---

Luxe is a coding agent for your terminal. It works in your project with the model you choose,
then walks you through what it changed so you can review it and open a pull request without leaving
the terminal.

New to Luxe? [Install](install.md) it, then follow the [Quickstart](quickstart.md). The rest of the
guide is reference, for when you need it.

## Find what you need

| To | Read |
| --- | --- |
| Connect a model, or switch between them | [Models and providers](providers.md) |
| Find your way around the screen | [The interface](interface.md) |
| Find a command or a key, or rebind one | [Commands and keys](commands.md) |
| Point the agent at a file, issue or skill | [Mentions](mentions.md) |
| Review what the agent changed | [Guided Review](guided-review.md) |
| Work from an issue, open or merge a pull request | [Git and GitHub](github.md) |
| Resume a session, or see what fills the context | [Sessions and context](sessions.md) |
| See what the agent can use | [Tools](tools.md) |
| Let the agent work through a plan on its own | [Autonomous runs](loop.md) |
| Change the theme, keys or statusline | [Configuration](configuration.md) |
| Give the agent your project's conventions | [Project context](project-context.md) |
| Add tools, skills or your own commands | [Extending Luxe](extending.md), [Recipes](recipes.md) |
| Control what the agent may do | [Security and permissions](security.md) |
| Look up a command, flag or environment variable | [Command line](cli.md), [Environment variables](environment.md) |
| Fix something that is not working | [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md) |

## Help

- **Help** (`/help`) lists every key for the screen you are on, with any you have rebound.
- `luxe doctor` checks which language servers, debuggers and tools Luxe can use on your machine.
- [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md) covers common problems and how to report a bug.
- Problems and questions: [GitHub issues](https://github.com/evanwhittaker/luxe/issues).

## Ask Luxe

This guide is built into Luxe, for the version you have installed. Ask the agent how to do
something in Luxe, such as *how do I add an MCP server?*, and it reads the answer from the guide
rather than guessing. You can read it yourself too:

```bash
luxe docs                  # every page
luxe docs hooks            # one page
luxe docs --search "on_ask"
```

## For agents

Every page is also plain markdown, at the same address with `.md` on the end:
`https://luxe.dev/docs/install.md`. [`llms.txt`](https://luxe.dev/llms.txt) lists every page with a
one-line summary, and [`llms-full.txt`](https://luxe.dev/llms-full.txt) is the whole guide in one
file. Inside Luxe, `luxe docs` serves the same pages offline.
@@@ page: install
---
title: "Install"
summary: "Install Luxe, check your setup, and pick a font."
order: 1
group: "Get started"
---

## Install

On macOS and Linux, the install script puts `luxe` in `~/.local/bin`, or in `$LUXE_INSTALL_DIR`
when it is set, and adds that to your `PATH`:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://luxe.dev/install.sh | sh
```

That address redirects to the script on the [latest
release](https://github.com/evanwhittaker/luxe/releases/latest), the one it built and attested. To
read it before running it, drop the `| sh`.

With Homebrew, on macOS or Linux:

```bash
brew install evanwhittaker/tap/luxe
```

With Cargo, which builds it, so you need Rust 1.89 or newer ([rustup](https://rustup.rs) installs
one):

```bash
cargo install --locked luxe-cli
```

On Windows, in PowerShell:

```powershell
powershell -c "irm https://luxe.dev/install.ps1 | iex"
```

[That script](https://luxe.dev/install.ps1) is two lines: it lets this PowerShell window run the
release's installer, which Windows' default execution policy would stop, then runs it. Nothing
about your policy is saved.

Any of them installs the `luxe` command; `luxe --version` checks it worked.

To update, run `luxe update`, or `/update` inside Luxe. Luxe checks once a day for a newer release
and says so on the start screen; see [Updates](configuration.md#updates) for how it updates and how
to turn the check off.

### Check a download

Every file on a release carries a build attestation, so you can confirm it came from this
repository's release workflow and nowhere else:

```bash
gh attestation verify luxe-cli-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.xz --repo evanwhittaker/luxe
```

## Build from source

```bash
git clone https://github.com/evanwhittaker/luxe.git
cd luxe
cargo build --release
./target/release/luxe --version
```

## Requirements

Luxe runs natively on Linux, macOS and Windows. Only a terminal and a model are required.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Terminal** | Any current terminal with UTF-8. On Windows, use Windows Terminal. |
| **Model** | An API key, a ChatGPT, Copilot or OpenRouter subscription, or a local server such as LM Studio or Ollama. See [Providers](providers.md). |
| **Git** | For reviewing changes and working in worktrees. Without a repository, Luxe runs with nothing to review. |
| **GitHub CLI** | Optional. `gh`, signed in, for issues and pull requests. |
| **A Nerd Font** | Optional, for icons. See [Fonts](#fonts). |

Luxe also uses these when they are installed:

- `ast-grep`, for structural search.
- A language server per language, for code intelligence. See [Code
  intelligence](tools.md#code-intelligence).
- A debug adapter per language, for the debugger. See [Debugger](tools.md#debugger).

## Check your setup

```bash
luxe doctor
```

`luxe doctor` lists the tools, language servers and debug adapters Luxe found, which ones work, and
how to install what is missing:

```
External programs
  ok    git        git
  ok    gh         git (pull requests)

Language servers
  ok    rust         rust-analyzer
  none  go           tried: gopls
        go install golang.org/x/tools/gopls@latest
```

## Fonts

Luxe draws its icons from a [Nerd Font](https://www.nerdfonts.com/) when your terminal has one.
Without one, it falls back to plain characters on its own, and every icon has a word beside it, so
nothing becomes unreadable.

The screenshots use **JetBrains Mono Nerd Font Mono**:

```bash
brew install --cask font-jetbrains-mono-nerd-font   # macOS
sudo pacman -S ttf-jetbrains-mono-nerd               # Arch
scoop install nerd-fonts/JetBrainsMono-NF-Mono       # Windows, after `scoop bucket add nerd-fonts`
```

Use the **Mono** build of a Nerd Font. The other build draws icons wider than one cell, so they
overlap the character after them. Set it in your terminal by its short family name:

```toml title="alacritty.toml"
[font]
normal = { family = "JetBrainsMono NFM" }
```

The short name matters on Linux desktops that pick their monospace font with a fontconfig rule,
such as Omarchy. Asking for the full name, `JetBrainsMono Nerd Font Mono`, can hand you the
desktop's font instead. To check what a name resolves to:

```bash
fc-match -f '%{file}\n' "JetBrainsMono NFM"
```

JetBrains Mono lacks six symbols Luxe draws (`ℹ︎ ↳︎ ↺︎ ⏸︎ ✔︎ ✖︎`), and your system fills them in
from another font. For every character from one face, use **IosevkaTerm** or **Adwaita Mono**:

```bash
brew install --cask font-iosevka-term-nerd-font    # "IosevkaTerm NFM"
brew install --cask font-adwaita-mono-nerd-font    # "AdwaitaMono Nerd Font Mono"
sudo pacman -S ttf-iosevka-nerd ttf-adwaitamono-nerd
scoop install nerd-fonts/IosevkaTerm-NF-Mono nerd-fonts/AdwaitaMono-NF-Mono
```

To use the wider icons anyway, set `"glyphs": "nerd_wide"` in
[`config.json`](configuration.md), and Luxe gives each icon two cells.

## On Windows

Install [Git for Windows](https://gitforwindows.org/). Luxe finds its `bash` even though it is not
on `PATH`, and the agent needs a POSIX shell for most commands. Without one, commands run through
`cmd.exe`, which handles `cargo test` or `npm run build` but not much else.

If WSL is installed, Luxe skips the `bash.exe` in `System32`, which would run commands inside Linux
against a different filesystem.

## Where Luxe keeps files

| | Linux and macOS | Windows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Configuration and credentials | `~/.config/luxe` | `%APPDATA%\luxe` |
| State | `~/.local/state/luxe` | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\luxe` |
| Cache | `~/.cache/luxe` | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\luxe` |

An `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, `XDG_STATE_HOME` or `XDG_CACHE_HOME` you have set wins on every platform.
`LUXE_CONFIG_DIR` moves every configuration file, API key and provider sign-in. `LUXE_STATE_DIR`
moves the state Luxe keeps for you: the model you last chose, MCP sign-ins, and the logs of
commands that only report, such as `luxe auth`.

Inside a project, Luxe keeps its sessions, logs and caches in `.luxe/`, with a `.gitignore` that
keeps all of it out of Git except the files a team may want to share: `permissions.json`,
`mcp.json`, `hooks.json` and `skills/`.
@@@ page: interface
---
title: "The interface"
summary: "The start screen, the conversation, the composer, the dock, the statusline and the preview."
order: 3
group: "Using Luxe"
---

![The dock beside the preview, showing one file's diff](images/interface-peek.svg)

This page names the keys for each part of the screen. All of them, and how to rebind them, are in
[Commands and keys](commands.md); `/help` lists the ones for the screen you are on, and the
**Command Palette** (`ctrl+k`) finds any command by name. Which editor and file manager open is in
[Environment variables](environment.md#integrations).

## The start screen

Luxe opens on a prompt. Type and press `enter` to ask in a new session, or choose a row from the
list under it with `↑`/`↓` and `enter`.

| Row | Opens |
| --- | --- |
| **Set up a provider** | Configuration. Leads the list, and takes `enter` on an empty prompt, until a provider is set up. |
| **Resume** | Your last session, named with its title and how long ago. Once a provider is set up, `enter` alone opens it. |
| **New session** | A fresh conversation |
| **Sessions…** | Every session in this project, searchable. `/sessions` opens it too, here or in a session. |
| **Review changes** | A [Guided Review](guided-review.md) of your uncommitted changes, when there are any |
| **Configuration** | Providers, credentials, [settings](configuration.md#settings) and config files, once a provider is set up |
| **Quit** | Leaves Luxe. `ctrl+c` does too, here and in a session, even mid-turn, unless a prompt or menu is open, which it answers instead. |
| **RECENT** | Your other recent sessions |

Typing narrows the list. The first row becomes **Ask in a new session**, and under it come the
sessions whose titles match, the commands that do, and a search through every session's transcript.
A session you open this way keeps what you typed in its composer. Once a draft reads as a prompt
(more than five words or 48 characters, a second line, a pasted chip or a mention), the list folds
away and `enter` asks.

`/` and `@` open the same command and [mention](mentions.md) pickers a session has, under the
prompt. A command chosen there either opens over the start screen, as `/model` and `/theme` do, or
starts a new session to run in.

![The start screen with a search typed](images/interface-launcher-typing.svg)

Every key is text here, so `esc` clears the prompt rather than quitting. `shift+tab`, or a click on
the prompt's title, switches between build and [plan mode](agent.md#plan-then-build) before you
start, and the session opens in the mode you chose. The statusline under it is the one the session
will have.

Nothing picks a model for you. Until you choose one, sending a message opens the model picker with
your message kept.

### Styles

```json title="~/.config/luxe/config.json"
{ "dashboard": { "style": "minimal" } }
```

`minimal` shows the prompt alone, and the list waits for `↓`. `"dashboard": false` skips the start
screen and opens a new session. **Start screen** in `/settings` sets the same key.

![The minimal start screen](images/interface-launcher-minimal.svg)

Luxe works on the project it was started in. To switch projects, `cd` there and run `luxe`.

## The conversation

Each tool call the agent makes is a card, showing what it did and how long it took. `ctrl+o` shows
every card's full output, and clicking a card opens it.

![A finished turn: three reads folded into one card, an edit with its diff, a test run and the reply](images/interface-turn.svg)

A shell command card is titled by what the agent says the command is for, such as "Run the forms
tests", with the first line of the command under it and the rest a click away. A test run through
the shell that fails shows its counts and what failed, the same as the `test` tool's card.

Three or more lookups from one message (`read`, `grep`, `glob`, `ast_grep` and the code intelligence
tools) fold into one card that lists what they looked at: the first five by name, or four and a
count of the rest. So do three or more calls in a row to one MCP server, with nothing shown between
them. Click a folded card to open it into one card per call, and click again to fold it. Edits,
commands, `git`, the todo list and anything that failed always keep their own card. `"conversation":
{ "tool_runs": "cards" }` turns folding off.

Tables in a reply fit the width they are drawn at. Narrower than the table, cells wrap inside their
columns; too narrow for that, each row is listed as `Header: value` lines.

Code blocks in a reply are highlighted for their language. Click the rule above a block to copy it.

| To | Key |
| --- | --- |
| Scroll | wheel, `ctrl+↑` / `ctrl+↓`, `pageup` / `pagedown` |
| Jump to the newest output | `ctrl+end` |
| Search the conversation | `ctrl+f` |
| Select the previous or next message | `alt+k` / `alt+j` |
| Copy the selected message | `alt+y` |
| Edit your last message and send it again | `alt+e` |
| Ask again, after the last answer | `alt+t` |
| Replace the last answer | `alt+g` |
| View the newest image full-window | `alt+i` |

## The composer

`enter` sends. `shift+enter` adds a line. Type `/` for [commands](commands.md) and `@` to
[mention](mentions.md) a file, skill, issue or other context.

The composer's title names the session's mode, **build** or **plan**. `shift+tab` or a click on the
title switches it; see [Plan, then build](agent.md#plan-then-build).

While the agent works, you can keep typing:

| Key | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `enter` | **Steer**: the message reaches the running turn between steps, without stopping it |
| `alt+enter` or `alt+q` | **Queue**: the message becomes the next turn, after this one ends |
| `alt+↑` | Bring waiting messages back into the composer to edit |
| `ctrl+esc` | Stop the turn. Waiting messages come back into the composer. |

A waiting message sits above the composer, marked `steering` or `queued`, until it is delivered.

`ctrl+v` or `shift+insert` pastes. Pasted text of three lines or more, or over 150 bytes, becomes a
`[Pasted 40 lines]` chip, and a pasted image becomes `[Pasted Image]`. Both are sent in full. A chip, like a mention, is deleted with one `backspace`.

The composer and every other text field take the usual line-editing keys:

| To | Key |
| --- | --- |
| Move by word | `ctrl+←` / `ctrl+→`, or `alt+←` / `alt+→` |
| Start or end of line | `home` / `end`, or `ctrl+a` / `ctrl+e` |
| Delete the word before or after | `alt+backspace` / `alt+delete` |
| Delete to the start of the line | `ctrl+u` |
| Select | `shift` with any move, or `alt+a` for everything |

On macOS, Option and Cmd with the arrows and `backspace` do the same in Ghostty, and in other
terminals with their natural text editing preset.

## The dock

The Context Dock is the column beside the conversation. It sits beside it on terminals 136 columns
or wider. On narrower ones it is hidden until you press `alt+d`, and then opens over the
conversation, or in its place below 80 columns.

| Section | Shows |
| --- | --- |
| **PROJECT** | The project, its branch, and the branch's pull request: `#138 · 1 failing · 2 threads` |
| **PLAN** | The agent's todo list, scrolled to what it is working on |
| **FILES** | The project as a tree, with what changed marked in it. Click a file to [preview](#preview) it. |
| **ELSEWHERE** | Files the session changed outside the project, when there are any |
| **MODEL** | The provider, model, thinking level and [mode](agent.md#plan-then-build). Click the model to change it, or the mode to switch it. |
| **SESSION** | Context used, tokens and cost, with what a review and compaction cost on rows of their own. A review's row shows its full cost once its guide or drafted summary is done. |

`alt+d` shows or hides the dock, and `/dock left` or `/dock right` moves it. To set it for good:

```json title="~/.config/luxe/config.json"
{
  "dock": { "mode": "auto", "position": "left" }
}
```

`mode` is `auto` (beside the conversation when there is room), `shown` or `hidden`.

Drag the line between the dock and the conversation to make the dock wider or narrower. It stays
that width the next time Luxe starts; double-click the line to put it back.

### Files

**FILES** is the project's tree. Dotfiles such as `.github` are in it; what `.gitignore` ignores is
not, until you ask for it. Folders on the way to a changed file open on their own, so the change is
in view; a changed file shows its letter (`M`, `A`, `D`, `?`) and its line counts, and a closed
folder with a change inside shows a dot. A folder holding only one folder is drawn as one row,
`crates/luxe-core/src`. `all ▾` on the heading opens a menu: show only what changed, or show the
ignored files too, drawn faint.

Click a folder to open or close it, and a file to [preview](#preview) it; the file showing is drawn
in the accent color. Right-click either for everything you can do with it.

The tree only reads. To move, rename or delete files, ask the agent, which goes through your
permissions and shows up in the review, or press `O` to open the folder in your file manager. A
terminal one such as yazi takes the screen until you quit it, as your editor does; the tree reads
its folders again when you come back.

`ctrl+t` moves the keyboard into the tree, and pressed again, into the file showing beside it.
`tab` trades the keyboard between the two, and `esc` hands it back to the composer.

| In the tree | Key |
| --- | --- |
| Move | `j` / `k`, or the arrows |
| Find a file by typing part of its path | `/` |
| Open a folder, or show a file | `enter` |
| Open a folder, or show a file and move into it | `l` |
| Close a folder, or go to its parent | `h` |
| Open in your editor | `o` |
| Open its folder in a file manager | `O` |
| Mention it in the composer | `@` |
| Copy its path | `y` |
| Only what changed, or everything | `a` |
| Show the ignored files, or hide them | `i` |
| Read the folders again | `R` |
| Back to the composer | `esc` |

Any other key goes to the composer, so you can start typing without leaving the tree first.

`/` filters the tree as you type. It searches the whole project, not just the open folders, and
matches the letters in order anywhere in the path, so `tuiview` finds `crates/luxe-tui/src/view.rs`.
The tree shows the best matches under the folders that hold them, with the matched letters lit.
The arrows move through them, and `enter` shows one. `esc` clears the filter and leaves the
cursor on the file you found. Files `.gitignore` ignores are never matched, even while the tree is
showing them.

## The statusline

The statusline is the bar under the composer. It carries the same model, context and cost the
dock does, so by default it shows only when the dock is not beside the conversation. That makes
`alt+d` a swap on a wide terminal: hiding the dock brings the statusline back, and showing it puts
the statusline away. `alt+s` or `/statusline show`, `hide` or `auto` changes that, and
`"statusline": { "visibility": "shown" }` keeps it. [Statusline modules](appearance.md#statusline)
sets what it shows.

## Preview

The **preview** (`ctrl+p`) shows one file in place of the conversation, with the dock and the
composer where they were, so you can reply about what you see. A changed file opens on its diff, and
`alt+m`, or **FILE** in the header, shows it whole; **DIFF** goes back. Any other file opens whole.
Click another file under `FILES` to switch; click the open one, or press `esc`, to go back.
`/preview src/app.rs` opens a given file.

To ask about part of a file, drag across its lines (or click one) and choose **ask about lines**
under them, or press `alt+l`. The composer gets `@[file:src/app.rs:40-52]`: the agent receives the
path and the lines, and reads them itself. Right-click the lines to copy them instead.

On a wide terminal the conversation stays beside the diff. The diff takes the width code needs,
about 134 columns in one column or 218 side by side, and the conversation gets the rest.
Drag the line between them to change the split, and double-click it to go back.

The preview is not a review: looking at a file does not count it as reviewed.

| In the preview | Key |
| --- | --- |
| Next or previous changed file | `alt+n` / `alt+p` |
| The whole file, or its diff | `alt+m` |
| Ask about the lines you picked | `alt+l` |
| Side by side, or one column | `ctrl+b` |
| Wrap long lines, or not | `alt+w` |
| Open the file in your editor, at the top line shown | `alt+o` |
| Open a [Guided Review](guided-review.md) of your changes, at this file | `ctrl+g` |
| Back to the conversation | `esc` |

With the keyboard in the file (`ctrl+t` twice, or `tab` from the tree), a cursor moves line by
line and the file scrolls to keep it in view. In a diff the same keys scroll.

| In the file | Key |
| --- | --- |
| Move the cursor | `j` / `k`, or the arrows; `space` / `pageup` a page, `ctrl+d` / `ctrl+u` half of one; `g` / `G` the ends |
| Select lines, like vim's visual-line mode: moves grow the pick, `o` moves its other end | `v` or `V` |
| Grow a pick by one line without the mode | `J` / `K`, or `shift` with the arrows |
| Ask about the pick, or the cursor's line | `enter` |
| Copy the pick, or the cursor's line | `y` |
| Open in your editor at the cursor | `o` |
| Back to the tree | `tab` or `h` |
| Drop the pick or leave visual mode, then back to the composer | `esc` |

## Mouse and clipboard

The wheel scrolls whatever is under the pointer, and a click acts on what you click. Drag any
scrollbar to scroll, or press anywhere on it to jump.

The lines between panes move: the dock's, the preview's, and the one beside a review's guide. A line
lights under the pointer; drag it to resize the pane beside it, or double-click it to put the pane
back to its own width. Luxe remembers the widths for next time.

Drag across the conversation or the composer to select, and the selection is copied when you let
go. Click a message to copy all of it. `ctrl+insert` or `ctrl+shift+c` copies a selection too.

Your terminal's own copy key reaches Luxe only if the terminal passes it through. Either hold
`shift` (`option` on macOS) while dragging, to make a selection the terminal copies itself, or let
the copy key fall through when the terminal has nothing selected. In Ghostty:

```ini title="ghostty config"
keybind = performable:control+insert=copy_to_clipboard
```

Luxe copies to the desktop clipboard, and over SSH through the terminal (OSC 52). Inside tmux,
that needs `set -g set-clipboard on`.

`/mouse off` hands the mouse back to the terminal for the session, and `"mouse": false` in
`config.json` starts with it off. `"conversation": { "scroll_lines": 5 }` sets how far a wheel
notch scrolls, from 1 to 20 lines (3 by default).
@@@ page: loop
---
title: "Autonomous runs"
summary: "Let the agent work through a phased plan on its own, with tests and a reviewer at each phase."
order: 12
group: "Using Luxe"
---

`luxe loop` runs the agent on its own, phase by phase through your plan. A phase only counts as done
once your tests pass and, if you set one up, a reviewer agrees.

## Write the plan

Put the plan in `PLAN.md` at the project root, one heading per phase.
[Plan mode](agent.md#plan-then-build) writes it in this shape for you, and when it is done, **Run
it as a loop** switches the session to build and tells you to run `luxe loop start`.

![Plan mode's plan written, asking what next: build here, in a fresh session, or run it as a loop](images/loop-plan-ready.svg)

```markdown title="PLAN.md"
# Word counts

## Phase 0 — Count words
Read a file and print its word count. Tests for an empty file and one line.

## Phase 1 — Count by line
...
```

The agent is given one phase at a time, and the reviewer judges it against the same section. A plan
without phase headings is worked on as a whole.

## Start a run

```bash
luxe loop start
```

| Command | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `luxe loop start` | Start a run in a new session, at the phase the last one reached |
| `luxe loop status` | Iteration, phase, whether it is running, and what it has cost |
| `luxe loop pause`, `luxe loop resume` | Pause, and clear a pause so `start` continues |
| `luxe loop stop` | Stop the run |
| `luxe loop phase` | Show the phase. `--set <n>` changes it. |
| `luxe loop fresh` | Reset the turn count, so the next `start` gets all of `--max-turns` again |

| Flag | Default | Does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--max-turns` | `50` | Most turns before the run stops. The count carries over when you start again; `luxe loop fresh` resets it. |
| `--compact-percent` | the `compaction.at` you set, else `75` | How full the usable context window gets before the session is summarized; see [Compaction](sessions.md#compaction) |
| `--pause-percent` | `90` | How full it gets before the run stops. Keep it above `--compact-percent`, and run `luxe loop start` to go on. |
| `--quiet` | | Print only the banner |

A run uses your session's model, or `--model`. Only one run at a time works in a project.

## Check each phase

When the agent says a phase is done, Luxe checks it before moving on:

1. **Your commands.** Each must pass.
2. **A reviewer**, if `gate.review` is on and the commands passed. It runs in a fresh session, so
   it judges the phase without the reasoning that produced it. It reads the phase's section of the
   plan, the diff and the command output, and can look around the code with read-only tools. It
   cannot edit.

```json title=".luxe/config.json"
{
  "gate": {
    "commands": [
      ["cargo", "nextest", "run", "--workspace"],
      ["cargo", "clippy", "--workspace", "--all-targets", "--", "-D", "warnings"]
    ],
    "timeout_secs": 600,
    "review": true
  }
}
```

The reviewer runs on the run's own model unless `reviewer.model` names another, which turns
`gate.review` on by itself. A local model building and a hosted one reviewing is a common pairing:
the review is a few calls per phase, the building is most of them. See
[A second opinion](agent.md#a-second-opinion).

Each command is a program and its arguments, run without a shell. For shell features, use
`["sh", "-c", "…"]`. A project's commands replace your global ones only when you start with
`--trust-project`. Otherwise they're ignored with a warning, and your global commands apply.

If a check fails, the findings go back to the agent as work and the phase does not advance. With
neither check set up, the agent's word is taken. The same checks apply before the run may finish.

A review is limited to 24 tool calls and 10 minutes. A phase only advances when the reviewer
approves it. If the reviewer cannot answer, has nothing to read, or refuses the same phase three
times, the loop pauses for you: fix what it needs and run `luxe loop start` again, or accept the
phase with `luxe loop phase --set <next>`.

## Watch a run

A run prints one line per step, timed from its start:

```text
      19s    write logstats.py
      49s    test python3 -m unittest -q
    1m09s  phase 0 claimed complete — running the gate
    1m31s  the acceptance commands passed — asking the reviewer
    2m34s  phase 0 accepted — now on phase 1
```

`luxe loop status` shows what it has cost, by model:

```text
  Spend this run:
    claude-sonnet-5: 3 calls, 26295 tokens
    qwen3.6-27b: 19 calls, 188660 tokens
```

The conversation is in `.luxe/sessions/`, the log in `.luxe/logs/luxe.log`, and the journal the
agent keeps in `.luxe/loop/PROGRESS.md`. Past 24 KB, the journal's older `##` sections move to
`PROGRESS.archive.md` beside it, and a line pointing there takes their place. The newest section
stays, unless it is the only one.

## When a tool asks permission

Nobody is there to answer, so a tool call that would ask you is allowed by default. To refuse those
calls instead, and tell the agent to find another way:

```json title="~/.config/luxe/config.json"
{ "agent": { "on_ask": "deny" } }
```

`--on-ask deny` does the same for one run. A project can set `deny` but not `allow`. Calls your
permission rules deny are refused either way. See [Security](security.md#when-you-step-away).
@@@ page: mcp
---
title: "MCP servers"
summary: "Give the agent tools from MCP servers: add one, sign in, and control what it may do."
order: 3
group: "Extend"
---

An [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server gives the agent new tools: a browser, a database,
your issue tracker. Luxe reaches every server through one `mcp` tool, so a server's tools cost
nothing in a request until the agent looks for them:

```text
mcp({ search: "screenshot" })                                    find tools by keyword or server
mcp({ tool: "chrome/take_screenshot" })                          one tool's parameters
mcp({ tool: "chrome/take_screenshot", args: "{\"format\":\"png\"}" })   call it
```

## Add a server

Add servers to `~/.config/luxe/mcp.json`. The `mcpServers` format other tools write works as it is:

```json title="~/.config/luxe/mcp.json"
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "chrome": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "chrome-devtools-mcp@latest"] },
    "linear": { "url": "https://mcp.linear.app/mcp", "auth": { "kind": "oauth" } }
  }
}
```

A server is a local program (`command` and `args`) or a remote address (`url`). Or from the command
line:

```bash
luxe mcp add --id chrome --name "Chrome" --command "npx -y chrome-devtools-mcp@latest"
luxe mcp list     # configured servers
luxe mcp tools    # every server's tools
luxe mcp remove --id chrome
```

`luxe mcp add` and `luxe mcp remove` change only the project's `.luxe/mcp.json`, so a server added
this way is a [project's server](#servers-a-project-brings), and one in your own `mcp.json` is
removed by editing that file. `luxe mcp list` starts nothing: it shows every configured server,
disabled ones included, and marks a project's entries `not started (project)`, with or without
`--trust-project`. In a session, `/mcp` shows each server, how it connects and its tools.

Luxe also reads `~/.config/mcp/mcp.json`, and a project's `.mcp.json` and `.luxe/mcp.json`. Where
two files name the same server, the project's wins.

### Server settings

| Key | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `command`, `args`, `env` | Start a local server. An `env` value can use `${VAR}` or `$env:VAR`; an unset one is empty, and Luxe logs which. |
| `url`, `headers` | Connect to a remote server. `headers` take `${VAR}` the same way. |
| `auth` | Sign in: see [below](#sign-in) |
| `lifecycle` | `lazy` (the default) connects on first use and disconnects when idle. `eager` connects at start; `keep_alive` stays connected. |
| `timeout_secs` | How long one call may take. 60 by default. A call that runs over stops the server; the next call starts it again. |
| `exclude_tools` | Tool names to hide from the agent |
| `enabled` | `false` turns a server off without removing it |

## Sign in

A remote server signs in with a token or with OAuth.

```json title="~/.config/luxe/mcp.json"
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "internal": {
      "url": "https://mcp.example.com/mcp",
      "auth": { "kind": "bearer", "token_env": "INTERNAL_MCP_TOKEN" }
    },
    "linear": { "url": "https://mcp.linear.app/mcp", "auth": { "kind": "oauth" } }
  }
}
```

For OAuth, sign in once in a browser, and Luxe refreshes the token from then on:

```bash
luxe mcp login --id linear
```

The agent never starts a sign-in. Tokens are kept in `~/.local/state/luxe/mcp-auth.json`, readable
only by you. With `LUXE_STATE_DIR` set they are kept there instead, so a moved state directory does
not share the default one's sign-ins. If that file stops being valid JSON, Luxe moves it to
`mcp-auth.json.bad` (or a dated name, if one is already there) rather than write over it, and you
sign in again.

A token only travels over `https`. A server with `auth` set whose `url` is plain `http` is refused
unless it is on this machine, and so is an OAuth endpoint, whether you wrote it or the server
described it. The server's metadata must also name itself as the issuer it was asked for.

Some providers, such as Asana, register each app and give you a client ID and secret. Add them,
with the redirect address you registered:

```json title="~/.config/luxe/mcp.json"
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "asana": {
      "url": "https://mcp.asana.com/v2/mcp",
      "auth": {
        "kind": "oauth",
        "client_id": "1209…",
        "client_secret": "${ASANA_MCP_CLIENT_SECRET}",
        "redirect_uri": "http://127.0.0.1:8765/callback"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

The redirect must be on `127.0.0.1`, `localhost` or `[::1]`, with the port you registered. A secret
or token can be written three ways:

- `${VAR}`: an environment variable. Programs the agent runs can read it too. If it is unset,
  sign-in stops and names the variable.
- `!command`: a command that prints it, such as `"!pass show asana/mcp-secret"`. It runs at sign-in
  and on each refresh, without a terminal, for up to 30 seconds. Only your own config can use this.
- The value itself, in a file only you can read (`chmod 600`).

Never put a secret in a project's `.mcp.json` or `.luxe/mcp.json`, which are shared with the
repository. [Asana, end to end](recipes.md#asana) walks through the whole setup.

## Point the agent at a server

In the `@` picker, the **MCP** tab lists each server with its state: `22 tools · signed in`, or
`not signed in — luxe mcp login --id linear`. Mentioning one, as in *@[mcp:asana] what is due this
week?*, sends the agent straight to it, with the names of its tools the first time.

## Control what a server may do

A tool call is checked by your permission rules, by its `server/tool` name:

```json title="~/.config/luxe/permissions.json"
{
  "permission": {
    "mcp": {
      "asana/get_*": "allow",
      "asana/create_*": "ask",
      "asana/delete_*": "deny"
    }
  }
}
```

The most specific rule wins. `deny` holds everywhere, even with `--yolo`. `ask` holds only when
someone is there to answer; in a headless or loop run it is allowed, unless `agent.on_ask` is
`deny`.

What a tool returns goes to your model provider, as the result of that call. Signing in and
`luxe mcp tools` send nothing to a model. If a server's data should only go to a provider your
organization approves, deny its tools until you are on one.

A server's descriptions and results are treated as information, never as instructions.

### Servers a project brings

A project's `.mcp.json` names programs that would run on your machine. Luxe starts a project's
servers in an interactive session, or with `--trust-project`, but not in a headless or loop run. To
decide for every run, set `lsp.project_servers` in your own config; see
[Tools](tools.md#a-server-the-project-installed).

`luxe mcp tools` and `luxe mcp login` do not ask whether to trust a project's servers. They skip
project servers unless you pass `--trust-project` or set `lsp.project_servers` to `always` in your
own config, and print the skipped server ids and how to allow them. Login refuses a skipped
server before contacting its OAuth endpoints. Your global `never` setting still wins over the
flag. Servers in your own config do not need project trust.
@@@ page: mention-sources
---
title: "Mention sources"
summary: "Add your own tab to the @ picker: Jira issues, Asana tasks, anything a program can list."
order: 4
group: "Extend"
---

A mention source adds a tab to the [`@` picker](mentions.md), filled by a program of yours. Pick a
row, and the agent receives the text your program gave for it.

## Add a source

```json title="~/.config/luxe/config.json"
{
  "mentions": [
    { "name": "Jira", "command": "jira-mentions", "icon": "\udb80\udf03" },
    { "name": "Asana", "kind": "task", "command": "asana-mentions", "args": ["--mine"] }
  ]
}
```

| Key | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | The tab's name |
| `command`, `args` | The program to run, found on `PATH` or given as a full path, and its arguments |
| `kind` | The mention's prefix, as in `@[task:1209…]`. By default the name in lowercase, with anything but letters and digits as `-`: `Jira Cloud` is `jira-cloud`. |
| `icon` | One Nerd Font glyph for the tab, as the character or a JSON escape. Without one, the tab shows a tag; without a Nerd Font, a plain mark. |

Sources are read from your own config only, since each one runs a program. Their tabs come after
Luxe's own: Files, Skills, GitHub and MCP, whose kinds `file`, `skill`, `github` and `mcp` are
taken. Two sources with the same kind get one tab, the first's.

## What the program prints

Luxe runs the program, in the project, the first time its tab opens, and lists what it prints: one
JSON object per line. The rows are kept until Luxe exits, so a new ticket, or a change to your
script, shows up the next time you start Luxe. The program has no terminal and no stdin, so it
cannot prompt for a sign-in.

```json
{"id": "PROJ-12", "label": "PROJ-12 Login fails on Safari", "detail": "In progress", "text": "Jira issue PROJ-12 \"Login fails on Safari\" (In progress) https://acme.atlassian.net/browse/PROJ-12"}
```

| Field | Is |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | Required, a string or a number, without `]`. Goes in the mention: `@[jira:PROJ-12]`. |
| `label` | Required. The row in the picker, up to 200 characters. |
| `detail` | Shown beside the label, up to 200 characters |
| `text` | What the agent receives, up to 600 characters. The label when missing. |

A program has 15 seconds and up to 500 rows. A line that is not JSON, is over 8 KB, or lacks an
`id` or `label` is skipped without a word, so a tab that stays empty usually means the output is
wrong. If the program fails, the tab shows the last line it wrote to stderr, or its exit status,
and it runs again the next time the tab opens.

Make `text` enough for the agent to find the rest: a title and a link, or an ID it can look up with
a CLI or an MCP server. A mention you type by hand, or one not picked since Luxe started, reaches
the agent as `Jira PROJ-12` alone. What a tracker says is other people's words, and it reaches your model
provider once you mention it.

## Example: your open Jira issues

```bash title="~/bin/jira-mentions"
#!/bin/sh
site=https://acme.atlassian.net
curl -sSf -u "$JIRA_USER:$JIRA_TOKEN" -G "$site/rest/api/3/search/jql" \
  --data-urlencode 'jql=assignee = currentUser() AND statusCategory != Done ORDER BY updated DESC' \
  --data-urlencode 'fields=summary,status' |
jq -c --arg site "$site" '.issues[] | {
  id: .key,
  label: "\(.key) \(.fields.summary)",
  detail: .fields.status.name,
  text: "Jira issue \(.key) \"\(.fields.summary)\" (\(.fields.status.name)) \($site)/browse/\(.key)"
}'
```

Make it executable (`chmod +x`), put it on your `PATH`, and add the Jira entry above. For Asana,
see [Recipes](recipes.md#asana). Or ask Luxe to write one for the tracker you use.
@@@ page: mentions
---
title: "Mentions"
summary: "Point the agent at a file, skill, issue, MCP server or your own tracker with `@`."
order: 5
group: "Using Luxe"
---

Type `@` at the start of a word in the composer to mention something. The picker opens on your
project's files; `tab` and `shift+tab` move between its tabs, typing filters, `↑`/`↓` move,
`enter` inserts the mention, and `esc` or a space closes it.

![The @ picker on its Files tab, changed files first](images/mentions-picker.svg)

| Tab | Lists |
| --- | --- |
| **Files** | Changed files first, then the rest of the project, 50 rows at most; type to narrow them. Respects `.gitignore`, and never lists `.git`, `target`, `node_modules` or `.cache`. |
| **Skills** | The [skills](skills.md) you have installed |
| **GitHub** | The pull requests and issues `/github` lists, through `gh` |
| **MCP** | The [MCP servers](mcp.md) this session can use, when there are any |
| Your own | Any [mention source](mention-sources.md) you add: Jira, Asana, a runbook index |

Dotfiles and files under dot-folders, such as `.gitignore` and `.github/`, are left off the first
list but show up when you type. Start with `.` to rank them with everything else.

The file list is read from disk each time the picker opens, every few seconds while the Files tab
shows, and when the agent changes files, so a file made or moved a moment ago is there. `ctrl+r` reads it
again on the spot.

## What the agent receives

A mention is a pointer, not a copy. Nothing is pasted into your message:

| Mention | The agent gets |
| --- | --- |
| `@[file:docs/plan.md]` | The path, to read when it needs to |
| `@[skill:gh-stack]` | The skill's name, to load with the `skill` tool |
| `@[file:src/app.rs:40-52]` | The path and those lines, from **ask about lines** in the [preview](interface.md#preview) |
| `@[github:acme/todo/issues/42]` | Its number, title, state and address, and the `git` tool call that reads it in full |
| `@[mcp:asana]` | The server to use, with the names of its tools the first time it is signed in and listing them |
| `@[jira:PROJ-12]` | The text your mention source gave for that row |

A mention typed by hand works too. The title and state of an issue, and a mention source's text,
come from a row you picked this session; for one you typed, the agent gets the address or
`Jira PROJ-12` and looks it up itself. A file or skill that does not exist is reported as missing.

So a large file never floods the conversation, and a file the agent then edits is never in it twice
in two versions. *Review @[file:docs/plan.md] and draft a plan* is enough: the agent opens the file
itself.

In the composer, a mention is one chip. The cursor steps over it, and one `backspace` deletes it.
In `/github`, `c` inserts a mention of the pull request or issue under the cursor.
@@@ page: project-context
---
title: "Project context"
summary: "Give the agent your project's conventions in AGENTS.md, and how Luxe finds the project."
order: 3
group: "Customize"
---

## AGENTS.md

Put your project's conventions in an `AGENTS.md` at its root, and the agent reads it at the start of
every session. In a project folder a `CLAUDE.md` works too; when both exist, `AGENTS.md` is used.
The global files below are read only by those names, so `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` is not.

Luxe reads, in order:

1. `~/.agents/AGENTS.md`, the file many people keep for every agent they use
2. `~/.config/luxe/agents.md`, for every project in Luxe
3. `AGENTS.md` at the top of the repository
4. One `AGENTS.md` per folder down to where you started Luxe

So a monorepo can keep shared rules at the root and package rules beside the code, and `luxe`
started in `packages/app` reads both. Nothing above the repository is read. Outside a repository,
only the folder you started in is, so an `AGENTS.md` in a parent folder never reaches a project it
was not written for.

The files are read once, when a session sends its first message, and every later request in the
session repeats that same text, which is what lets the provider reuse its cache. An edit reaches
the agent in the next session: `/new`, or resuming one. If you switch Git branches mid-session, the
agent is told with your next message.

**Project context** lists every file a turn reads, and says whose rules each one carries:
**global**, **project** or **folder** context. Type `context` on the start screen and open it.
`enter` opens a file in your editor, or creates one from a template. The template's guidance is in
comments, which Luxe removes and reports, so replace them with your own lines.

### Duplicates

A file the walk reaches twice is read once. That covers a symbolic link, such as
`~/.config/luxe/agents.md` pointing at `~/.agents/AGENTS.md`, and a file that is a byte-for-byte
copy of an earlier one. The context list shows the copy as *read once*.

Two files that say mostly the same thing are both read, because only you can say which sentence
should stay. Keep rules that apply everywhere in one global file, and the project's own rules in its
`AGENTS.md`.

```markdown title="AGENTS.md"
# AGENTS.md

- Run `pnpm test` before calling work done; `pnpm lint --fix` formats.
- Database changes go through a migration in `db/migrations/`, never by hand.
- The API returns errors as `{ "error": { "code", "message" } }`. Keep it that way.
- The current spec is in `docs/SPEC.md`. Read it before planning; skip it for small fixes.
```

### Keep it short

The file is part of every request, and a long one is followed less carefully, not more. For each
line, ask: would a capable model get this wrong without being told, and would that cost something?
Commands, pitfalls and conventions that differ from the usual pass. Directory layouts, dependency
lists and architecture overviews do not; the agent reads those from the code.

- A rule for one part of the tree goes in an `AGENTS.md` beside that code.
- A procedure the agent needs only sometimes goes in a [skill](skills.md).
- A plan, spec or design document stays a file. Name it in `AGENTS.md`, as above, and the agent
  reads it when the work calls for it.

An `AGENTS.md` over 24,000 characters is cut off, with a note telling the agent to read the rest of
the file itself.

### What Luxe removes

Two kinds of text are removed from `AGENTS.md` and skill files before the agent sees them, because
neither is visible to someone reviewing the file:

- Comments outside code blocks: HTML comments, `<!-- … -->`, and link definitions used as
  comments, such as `[//]: # (…)`
- Invisible Unicode: tag characters, supplementary variation selectors, bidirectional overrides,
  and soft hyphens and other marks that draw nothing, written as characters or as references
  such as `&#x202E;`

A file that repeats one link label so often that Luxe cannot check every definition is left out
entirely. For an `AGENTS.md`, Luxe says what it removed or left out when it starts; a skill file is
cleaned without a notice.

## Where the project begins

Luxe works on one project, found by walking up from where you started it:

1. Inside a repository (`.git`, `.jj` or `.hg`), the nearest folder with a `.luxe/` in it, up to
   the top of the repository
2. Otherwise, the top of the repository
3. Outside any repository, the folder you are in

So `luxe` started in `crates/parser/src` opens the whole repository, with its sessions, plan and
reviews. The walk stops at your home folder. A Git worktree is its own project.

To keep a package of a monorepo separate, give it a `.luxe/`:

```bash
mkdir -p packages/app/.luxe
```

The package keeps its own sessions and still reads the `AGENTS.md` at the top of the repository.

Outside a repository, a `.luxe/` claims only its own folder. Luxe writes one wherever it runs, so
starting it once in `~/.config` does not make `~/.config/herdr` part of that project.
@@@ page: providers
---
title: "Models and providers"
summary: "Sign in to a provider, choose a model and thinking level, and run local models."
order: 9
group: "Using Luxe"
---

## Sign in

Open **Configuration** (on the start screen, or `/config`) and choose how to connect. When a
provider connects, the model picker opens.

| Option | For |
| --- | --- |
| **Sign in to a subscription** | ChatGPT Plus or Pro, GitHub Copilot, or OpenRouter (which signs you in and creates a key) |
| **Add an API key** | Any provider below |
| **Connect a local or custom model** | LM Studio, Ollama, Azure, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint |
| **Edit configuration files** | `config.json`, `models.json`, `auth.json` and `keybindings.json`, in `$EDITOR` |

From the command line:

```bash
luxe auth login                          # choose a provider from a list
luxe auth login anthropic                # or name one
luxe auth login openai --stdin < key.txt # read the key from a file or a pipe
luxe auth list                           # every provider, and how each is configured
luxe auth status                         # credential type, where it came from, when it expires
luxe auth logout openai                  # remove a stored credential
```

In a session, `/login`, `/logout` and `/auth` do the same.

Signing in checks the key with one request for the provider's model list, and gives up on an
endpoint that stops answering after `LUXE_STREAM_START_TIMEOUT` seconds. Typing an endpoint that is
plain `http://` and not on this machine works, with a warning that the key will cross the network
unencrypted.

### Providers

| Provider | ID | Environment variable |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OpenAI | `openai` | `OPENAI_API_KEY` |
| ChatGPT Plus or Pro | `openai-codex` | subscription only |
| Anthropic | `anthropic` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` |
| GitHub Copilot | `github-copilot` | `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN` |
| OpenRouter | `openrouter` | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` |
| Google Gemini | `google` | `GEMINI_API_KEY` or `GOOGLE_API_KEY` |
| xAI | `xai` | `XAI_API_KEY` |
| DeepSeek | `deepseek` | `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` |
| Groq | `groq` | `GROQ_API_KEY` |
| Cerebras | `cerebras` | `CEREBRAS_API_KEY` |
| Mistral | `mistral` | `MISTRAL_API_KEY` |
| Alibaba DashScope | `dashscope` | `DASHSCOPE_API_KEY` |
| Z.AI | `zai` | `ZAI_API_KEY` |
| Moonshot AI | `moonshotai` | `MOONSHOT_API_KEY` |
| Together AI | `togetherai` | `TOGETHER_API_KEY` |
| Fireworks AI | `fireworks` | `FIREWORKS_API_KEY` |
| NVIDIA NIM | `nvidia` | `NVIDIA_API_KEY` |
| Vercel AI Gateway | `vercel` | `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` |
| Microsoft Foundry | `foundry-openai`, `foundry-anthropic`, `foundry-completions` | `FOUNDRY_API_KEY` |
| Azure OpenAI | `azure` | `AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY` |
| LM Studio | `lmstudio` | none |
| Ollama | `ollama` | none |
| Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint | `custom` | |

A provider's own variable works without signing in; when you have signed in too, the sign-in is
used. Anthropic and Google take API keys only: their terms do not allow their subscriptions to be
used from other programs.

GitHub Copilot serves Claude through Anthropic's Messages API, its newer GPT, Grok and MAI models
only through its Responses API, and the rest through chat completions. Copilot says which model
takes which, and Luxe sends each one where it belongs. Claude goes to Messages even though chat
completions would take it, because only Messages keeps its thinking, its effort level and the
prompt cache for the whole conversation. The models offered are your plan's own, kept current each
time the sign-in refreshes. Signing in turns on any model your plan offers that you have not been
asked about yet; one you turned off stays off.

### Where credentials are kept

Credentials are stored in `~/.config/luxe/auth.json` (`%APPDATA%\luxe\auth.json` on Windows),
readable only by you. Subscriptions refresh on their own. A key can be the key itself, an
environment variable, or a command whose output is the key, so a password manager works:

```json title="~/.config/luxe/auth.json"
{
  "openai": { "type": "api_key", "key": "sk-..." },
  "anthropic": { "type": "api_key", "key": "!op read op://vault/anthropic/credential" }
}
```

A command runs each time a request needs the key.

## Choose a model

`/model` opens the model picker: every model your providers can serve, configured providers first.
Type to search. The session carries on with the new model, even across providers, and Luxe
remembers your choice for next time.

From the command line, `--model` takes a model ID, or `provider/id` to pick the provider too:

```bash
luxe --model anthropic/claude-opus-5
```

To see what Luxe knows about a model, or list what you can use:

```bash
luxe models show anthropic/claude-opus-5   # context window, output limit, thinking levels, price
luxe models list --provider anthropic      # every model; * is active, + is configured
luxe models refresh --force                # update the model catalog now
```

Luxe ships with the [models.dev](https://models.dev) catalog built in and refreshes it in the
background, so a model released after your copy of Luxe still has the right context window and
price.

## Thinking

`/thinking` sets how hard the model reasons before answering: **Off**, **Minimal**, **Low**,
**Medium**, **High**, **XHigh** or **Ultra**. Levels the model does not support are grayed out.
`--thinking high` sets it at launch.

Luxe remembers the level per model, since `high` on a frontier model and on a small local one cost
very different amounts of time. To give a model its own starting level:

```json title="~/.config/luxe/models.json"
{
  "models": {
    "lmstudio/qwen3.8-27b": { "thinking": "medium" }
  }
}
```

The picker marks that level `default`. `/thinking` can still change it during a session.

## Subscriptions

Usage on a ChatGPT or Copilot subscription is counted in full but never added to what you spent.
`/cost` shows what it would have cost at API prices, as
`plan ≈$0.42 of usage over 12 calls, covered by your subscription`. On a
ChatGPT plan, the statusline shows how much of the plan is used, such as `12% weekly`, and `/cost`
shows when it resets. On a Copilot plan it shows the month's allowance the same way, such as `19%
monthly`.

Luxe prices Copilot usage at Copilot's per-token rates, so the figure matches what Copilot reports
for each request. A Copilot plan billed by the token spends its monthly allowance at those rates.

A ChatGPT subscription serves its own set of models, different from OpenAI's API, and `/model`
lists exactly those.

## Local models

**Connect a local or custom model** asks for the endpoint (blank takes the default) and records it
in `~/.config/luxe/models.json`. No credential is needed.

| Server | Default endpoint |
| --- | --- |
| LM Studio | `http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1` |
| Ollama | `http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1` |

The picker lists the models your server has loaded, asked fresh each time it opens. Embedding and
reranking models are left out.

For reasoning controls, chat templates and sampling settings on a local server, see
[Custom providers](custom-providers.md).

## Microsoft Foundry

One Foundry resource and key serve three APIs, which Luxe treats as three providers. Signing in to
one configures all three:

```bash
luxe auth login foundry
```

It asks for the resource name, its endpoint, or a deployment's **Target URI**, and the key. Then
choose a model with the provider that serves it:

| Provider | Serves | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `foundry-openai` | OpenAI's models | `luxe --model foundry-openai/gpt-5.6-terra` |
| `foundry-anthropic` | Claude | `luxe --model foundry-anthropic/claude-sonnet-5` |
| `foundry-completions` | DeepSeek, Grok, Llama, Mistral, Phi and Cohere | `luxe --model foundry-completions/deepseek-v4-pro` |

`/model` lists what your resource has deployed, not every model Azure offers. Luxe asks the
resource for its deployments when you sign in and again each time you open `/model`, and sorts them
onto the right provider by the model each one runs. `luxe models refresh` asks too. If a resource
cannot list its deployments, `/model` shows Azure's catalog marked `unverified`, and you can
[list them yourself](custom-providers.md#choose-which-deployments-luxe-offers).

Use a deployment's name as the model ID, whatever it is called. For keyless sign-in with Microsoft
Entra ID, see [Custom providers](custom-providers.md#keyless-sign-in-with-microsoft-entra-id).

## When a provider stalls

Luxe waits 60 seconds for a provider to start answering, and 180 seconds between parts of a reply.
If a provider is overloaded, rate limited or unreachable before it has sent anything, Luxe tries
again after 2, 4 and 8 seconds, showing `retrying (2/3)` above the composer. Once a reply has
started, a failure ends the turn rather than paying for the reply twice. A bad key or a refused
request is not retried.

| Variable | Default | Sets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `LUXE_STREAM_START_TIMEOUT` | `60` | Seconds to wait for a reply to start. `0` waits forever. |
| `LUXE_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT` | `180` | Seconds a reply may go quiet. `0` waits forever. |
| `LUXE_PROVIDER_RETRIES` | `3` | Tries after the first. `0` never retries. |
@@@ page: quickstart
---
title: "Quickstart"
summary: "From first launch to a reviewed pull request."
order: 2
group: "Get started"
---

This walks through one change from start to finish: connect a model, ask for something, review
what the agent did, and open a pull request.

## 1. Start Luxe in your project

```bash
cd your-project
git switch -c category-enum    # a branch for the work, so it can become a pull request
luxe
```

Reviewing changes and opening a pull request need a Git repository. A pull request also needs a
branch other than the one it merges into; `luxe --worktree` makes one for you, in a
[worktree](github.md#work-in-a-worktree) of its own.

The first time, Luxe asks four questions: a theme, a provider, which tools the agent can use, and
what Luxe opens on. Each one previews or explains itself, and `enter` moves on. `s` skips setup and
keeps none of the answers, though a provider you signed in to stays signed in. Your answers go to
`~/.config/luxe/config.json`, and `/settings` or `luxe init` changes them later.

![Setup, on its theme step](images/quickstart-setup.svg)

After that, Luxe opens on the start screen: a prompt, with your last session, your other sessions
and **Configuration** listed under it, or **Set up a provider** first if you have none yet. Type to ask something or to find a session or a command, or
use `↑`/`↓` and `enter` to open a row.

![The start screen](images/quickstart-dashboard.svg)

## 2. Connect a model

If you skipped the provider question, the start screen leads with **Set up a provider**. Open it
and pick one:

| Option | For |
| --- | --- |
| **Sign in to a subscription** | ChatGPT Plus or Pro, GitHub Copilot, OpenRouter |
| **Add an API key** | OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Groq and others |
| **Connect a local or custom model** | LM Studio, Ollama, Azure, any OpenAI-compatible endpoint |

![Configuration, before a provider is set up](images/quickstart-configuration.svg)

When it connects, the model picker opens. Choose a model, and change it any time with `/model`.

An API key in your environment works too. Luxe finds `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`,
`GEMINI_API_KEY` and the rest, and offers that provider's models. To sign in from a script or a
machine without the interface, use the CLI:

```bash
luxe auth login                       # choose a provider from a list
luxe auth login anthropic --stdin < key.txt
luxe auth list                        # every provider and how it is configured
```

Credentials are stored in `~/.config/luxe/auth.json`, readable only by you. See
[Providers](providers.md) for every option.

## 3. Ask for something

Type what you want on the start screen and press `enter`: it starts a new session and sends it.
`shift+enter` adds a line.

```
a notification's category is a free-form string, so a typo compiles; make it an enum
```

The agent reads, edits and runs commands, and each step appears as a card. Click a card to see its
full output, or press `ctrl+o` for every card's; `ctrl+esc` stops the turn. You can keep typing while it works:
a message sent mid-turn reaches the agent between steps, without stopping it.

![A turn in progress](images/quickstart-turn.svg)

**Changes** (`ctrl+p`) shows the diff so far, beside the conversation on a wide terminal and in its
place on a narrow one.

## 4. Review the change

Press `ctrl+g` to start a **Guided Review**. Luxe writes a guide to the change, split into
chapters, each with what changed, why, and how it was checked, next to the code. When
`review ready` shows above the prompt, press `ctrl+g` again to open it.

![Guided Review](images/quickstart-review.svg)

| Key | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `space` | Next |
| `c` | Comment on the line under the cursor |
| `a` | Ask the agent about it |
| `alt+enter` | Finish the review |
| `?` | Every key in the review |

Comments go to the agent as work to do when you finish with **Request fixes**.

## 5. Open a pull request

This needs the GitHub CLI, `gh`, signed in (`gh auth login`): **Open pull request** is offered once
`gh` says the branch has none. Finish the review (`alt+enter`) and choose it. Luxe drafts the title
and description from the review. The heading says what happens before it opens, such as
"commits and pushes first". The pull request pictured came from a session that took up an issue
([`luxe --issue 123`](github.md#start-from-an-issue)), so its branch is named for the issue and its
description closes it.

![Opening a pull request](images/quickstart-pull-request.svg)

Press `t` or `e` to edit the title or description, `d` to open it as a draft, and `enter` to open
it.

## 6. Come back later

**Resume**, the first row on the start screen, picks up your last session. From the command line:

```bash
luxe -c                    # the most recent session in this project
luxe sessions list         # this project's sessions, newest first
luxe --resume <id>         # a specific one
```

## Next

- [The interface](interface.md): the dock, the statusline, the Command Palette and every command.
- [Guided Review](guided-review.md): reviewing someone else's pull request, and answering review
  threads on yours.
- [Configuration](configuration.md): themes, keys and the statusline.
- [Project context](project-context.md): give the agent your project's conventions in `AGENTS.md`.
@@@ page: recipes
---
title: "Recipes"
summary: "Extensions put together: Asana, subagents, a classifier guard, Herdr, and a local model."
order: 8
group: "Extend"
---

## Asana

Two ways to bring Asana in, and they work together: its MCP server, so the agent can read and update
tasks, and a mention source, so you can point at one task with `@`.

### The MCP server

Asana registers each app, so each person makes one of their own.

1. **Register an MCP app** in Asana's developer console (**My apps**). Set its redirect URL to
   `http://127.0.0.1:8765/callback`, and leave **This is a native or command-line app** unchecked.
   Share it with your workspace. Your organization may need an admin to approve it.
2. **Keep the secret in your environment.** In `~/.zshrc` or `~/.bashrc`, then open a new
   terminal:

   ```bash
   export ASANA_MCP_CLIENT_SECRET='…'
   ```

3. **Add the server**, with your app's client ID, and hide the tools Asana marks as internal:

   ```json title="~/.config/luxe/mcp.json"
   {
     "mcpServers": {
       "asana": {
         "url": "https://mcp.asana.com/v2/mcp",
         "auth": {
           "kind": "oauth",
           "client_id": "1209…",
           "client_secret": "${ASANA_MCP_CLIENT_SECRET}",
           "redirect_uri": "http://127.0.0.1:8765/callback"
         },
         "exclude_tools": [
           "get_project_internal", "search_objects_internal", "log_widget_event",
           "create_task_confirm", "save_task_changes_confirm", "create_project_confirm",
           "create_project_confirm_populate", "save_project_changes_confirm"
         ]
       }
     }
   }
   ```

4. **Sign in** and check what you can use:

   ```bash
   luxe mcp login --id asana
   luxe mcp tools
   ```

5. **Decide what the agent may do.** Task names and comments go to your model provider when a tool
   returns them. To let reads through and ask before anything changes:

   ```json title="~/.config/luxe/permissions.json"
   {
     "permission": {
       "mcp": {
         "asana/create_*": "ask",
         "asana/update_*": "ask",
         "asana/delete_*": "ask",
         "asana/add_*": "ask"
       }
     }
   }
   ```

   If Asana's data may only go to a provider your organization approves, use
   `"asana/*": "deny"` until you are on one. In a headless or loop run, make the writes `deny`:
   nobody is there to answer an `ask`.

6. **Use it:** *@[mcp:asana] what is due this week?*

### Your tasks in the `@` picker

This needs a personal access token (**My apps → Personal access tokens**), since the MCP sign-in's
token works only for the MCP server. Your workspace's ID is in
`https://app.asana.com/api/1.0/workspaces`, read with the same token.

```bash title="~/bin/asana-mentions"
#!/bin/sh
curl -sSf -H "Authorization: Bearer $ASANA_PAT" -G https://app.asana.com/api/1.0/tasks \
  --data-urlencode assignee=me --data-urlencode "workspace=$ASANA_WORKSPACE" \
  --data-urlencode completed_since=now --data-urlencode limit=100 \
  --data-urlencode opt_fields=name,due_on,permalink_url |
jq -c '.data[] | (if .due_on then "due \(.due_on)" else "no due date" end) as $due | {
  id: .gid,
  label: .name,
  detail: $due,
  text: "Asana task \"\(.name)\" (\($due)) \(.permalink_url)"
}'
```

```json title="~/.config/luxe/config.json"
{ "mentions": [{ "name": "Asana", "command": "asana-mentions" }] }
```

A task you pick goes in as `@[asana:1209…]` and reaches the agent as its name, due date and link,
and the agent can look it up through the MCP server. See [Mention sources](mention-sources.md).

## Subagents

A subagent is a separate context that does one job and returns a summary, which is what a headless
Luxe run is:

```bash
luxe --headless --read-only --model openai/gpt-5.6 --format json \
```
