```bash
  -p "review src/parser.rs for edge cases" |
  jq -rs 'map(select(.type == "message" and .text != "")) | last.text'
```

`--read-only` keeps the subagent from changing anything, and `--model` lets it be a different model
from the one doing the work. The `jq` filter keeps the last message with text in it, which is the
summary. For a review of your own uncommitted work, [`/review`](agent.md#a-second-opinion) does
this without the wrapper.

To let the agent start one itself, wrap that command in an MCP server with a
`delegate(task, model)` tool. Then:

- Rule it like any tool: `"mcp": { "delegate/*": "ask" }` in `permissions.json` puts each one in
  front of you.
- Give the server a `timeout_secs` longer than a review takes. A call gets 60 seconds by default,
  and one that runs out stops the subagent.
- Return the subagent's stderr when it fails, so the agent sees why.
- Give a subagent that writes its own worktree, with `git worktree add`, so it stays out of yours.

Luxe refuses to nest more than two levels deep, since an agent that starts two subagents per turn
would multiply fast. `LUXE_MAX_DEPTH` raises the limit.

## A guard that asks a model

A `BeforeToolUse` [hook](hooks.md) can ask a small classifier model whether a command is
destructive, and ask you when it might be. This one calls a typed decision model running on your
own machine, and the request follows that model's API; any model that returns a probability works.

```bash title="~/.config/luxe/hooks/risk-gate.sh"
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
command=$(jq -r '.ToolUse.args.command')

risk=$(jq -n --arg c "$command" '{
    state: { command: $c },
    questions: { destructive: { type: "noul",
      instructions: "Would running this command cause irreversible data loss?" } }
  }' |
  curl -sS --max-time 2 "${DECISION_URL:-http://localhost:8000}/v1/systemone" \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data @- |
  jq -r '.answers.destructive.noul')

if awk "BEGIN{exit !($risk > 0.8)}"; then
  jq -n --arg r "scored $risk for irreversible data loss" '{decision:"ask", reason:$r}'
else
  echo '{"decision":"allow"}'
fi
```

```json title="~/.config/luxe/hooks.json"
{
  "BeforeToolUse": [
    {
      "matcher": "bash",
      "command": ["/home/you/.config/luxe/hooks/risk-gate.sh"],
      "timeout_ms": 2500,
      "on_timeout": "ask"
    }
  ]
}
```

- **It asks rather than blocks.** A hook can only make a call harder, so the worst a wrong answer
  costs is a prompt.
- **It adds to your rules, not replaces them.** Keep what must always hold in
  [`permissions.json`](security.md).
- **It runs before every matching call.** The `matcher` keeps it off `read` and `grep`; narrow it
  further, such as `{ "bash": "rm *" }`, to cost less.
- **`on_timeout: "ask"`** puts the question to you if the classifier is down.
- **Nobody answers in a headless run**, so its `ask` is allowed there. Use `--on-ask deny`, or
  `"hook_ask": "deny"` in `permissions.json`, to make it hold.

## Run Luxe in Herdr

[Herdr](https://herdr.dev) keeps coding agents in panes and shows which ones are working, waiting
on you, or done. Luxe reports its state to Herdr on its own when it runs in a Herdr pane:
**working** during a turn, **blocked** when it needs you, and **done** when the turn ends.

```bash
curl -fsSL https://herdr.dev/install.sh | sh
herdr
luxe        # in a pane
```

To let the agent drive Herdr, such as splitting panes or starting other agents, add Herdr's skill:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.config/luxe/skills/herdr
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ogulcancelik/herdr/master/SKILL.md \
  -o ~/.config/luxe/skills/herdr/SKILL.md
```

`LUXE_HERDR=0` or `{ "herdr": false }` in Luxe's config turns the reporting off.

### Luxe colors in Herdr

Herdr has no theme files — it takes a built-in theme plus per-token overrides. This is Luxe's
own palette in those tokens, so the pane and the multiplexer around it read as one program:

```toml title="~/.config/herdr/config.toml"
[theme]
name = "vesper"          # the closest built-in; every token below is overridden anyway

[theme.custom]
accent        = "#ddc084"  # champagne, the one color Luxe leads with
text          = "#e4dfd6"
subtext0      = "#97938c"
overlay0      = "#4d4a45"
overlay1      = "#97938c"
sidebar_bg    = "#12100e"  # the base surface, same as Luxe's background
panel_bg      = "#12100e"  # the tab bar sits on it too, so the chrome is one field
surface0      = "#201e1a"
surface1      = "#2e2b27"
surface_dim   = "#201e1a"
active_row_bg = "#201e1a"  # the current space, at rest
selection_bg  = "#2e2b27"  # the Navigate cursor, which should be the brighter of the two
mauve         = "#d2a5cd"  # branch names
yellow        = "#ddc084"  # working — an agent at work glows in the accent
green         = "#81caa0"  # idle / done
red           = "#e68485"  # blocked, needs you
peach         = "#faaa51"  # interrupted
blue          = "#85c7d7"  # Luxe has one cool hue, so blue and teal share it
teal          = "#85c7d7"

[ui]
accent = "#ddc084"         # borders and navigation chrome, which read off their own key
```

Reload it in place with `prefix+shift+r`, or `herdr server reload-config`. For any of the other
[themes](appearance.md) Luxe ships, the hexes are in its theme file and the token names above do
not change.

The one token worth a second thought is `panel_bg`: Herdr draws the active tab as `panel_bg` text
on an `accent` fill, so it has to stay dark enough to read there. Lifting it to `#201e1a` gives the
tab bar a surface of its own if you prefer the chrome delineated.

## A local model in LM Studio

1. Load a model in LM Studio and start its server.
2. In Luxe, open **Configuration** and choose **Connect a local or custom model**, then
   **LM Studio**. Leave the endpoint blank for the default.
3. Choose the model in the picker that opens.

LM Studio ignores the chat-template settings Luxe sends a local server by default, so for
thinking levels to reach the model, send them as `reasoning_effort`, and start each session at a
sensible level. Connecting already wrote an `lmstudio` provider to `models.json`, so add these keys
to it rather than replacing the file:

```json title="~/.config/luxe/models.json"
{
  "providers": {
    "lmstudio": { "compat": { "thinking_format": "openai" } }
  },
  "models": {
    "lmstudio/qwen3.8-27b": { "reasoning": true, "thinking": "medium" }
  }
}
```

[Custom providers](custom-providers.md) covers samplers and request formats.
@@@ page: rpc
---
title: "The RPC protocol"
summary: "Drive Luxe from your own program: an editor plugin, a dashboard, or a front end of your own."
order: 7
group: "Extend"
---

`luxe --rpc` runs Luxe without its interface and speaks JSON over stdin and stdout, one object per
line. Use it to build an editor plugin, a dashboard, a CI adapter, or a whole new front end, in any
language.

```bash
luxe --rpc        # takes the usual flags: --model, --permission-mode, -c, --resume
luxe --rpc --github-writes   # also lets your client publish to GitHub
```

A client is trusted like the interface it replaces: it answers permission prompts, and it cannot
loosen any permission rule. There is no network listener; your client is the process that started
Luxe.

## A session

```text
→  {"kind":"ready","content":{"protocol_version":2,"luxe_version":"0.1.0","session_id":"…","cwd":"/work/app","github_writes":false}}
→  {"kind":"state_changed","content":{"model":{…},"streaming":false,"mode":"build","thinking":"off"}}
←  {"kind":"submit_user_message","content":{"text":"what does this repo do?"}}
→  {"kind":"tool_started","content":{"call_id":"call_1","name":"read"}}
→  {"kind":"token_delta","content":{"block":0,"delta":"It is "}}
→  {"kind":"turn_usage","content":{"prompt_tokens":5018,"completion_tokens":26,"cost_usd":0.0258,…}}
→  {"kind":"turn_ended","content":{"reason":"end_turn"}}
←  {"kind":"close"}
```

Every frame is `{"kind": …, "content": …}`, and a frame with no payload leaves out `content`.
`ready` always comes first: check its `protocol_version` and refuse a number you do not know.

## A client

```python title="client.py"
import json, subprocess

luxe = subprocess.Popen(["luxe", "--rpc"], stdin=subprocess.PIPE,
                        stdout=subprocess.PIPE, text=True, bufsize=1)

def send(kind, content=None):
    frame = {"kind": kind} | ({"content": content} if content is not None else {})
    luxe.stdin.write(json.dumps(frame) + "\n")
    luxe.stdin.flush()

for line in luxe.stdout:
    event = json.loads(line)
    kind, body = event["kind"], event.get("content")

    if kind == "ready":
        assert body["protocol_version"] == 2, "unsupported protocol"
        send("submit_user_message", {"text": "What does this project do?"})
    elif kind == "token_delta":
        print(body["delta"], end="", flush=True)
    elif kind == "tool_started":
        print(f"\n[{body['name']}]")
    elif kind == "permission_requested":
        send("respond_permission", {"id": body["id"], "reply": "once"})
    elif kind == "question_asked":
        send("answer_question", {"id": body["id"], "reply": {"answered": ["yes"]}})
    elif kind == "action_rejected":
        print(f"\n! refused {body.get('kind')}: {body['reason']}")
    elif kind == "turn_ended":
        print()
        send("close")
    # Ignore everything else, so the client keeps working with newer versions of Luxe.
```

Three rules make a working client: read `ready` first, answer both kinds of prompt, and ignore
what you do not recognize.

## Actions

| `kind` | `content` | Does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `submit_user_message` | `{"text": "…", "images": [{"data": "<base64>", "mime": "image/png", "name": null}]}` | Start a turn. `images` is optional. |
| `steer_turn` | `{"text": "…"}` | Reach the running turn between tool calls, without ending it. With no turn running, starts one. |
| `withdraw_steering` | | Drop steering messages not yet delivered |
| `cancel` | | Stop the turn |
| `edit_resend` | `{"text": "…"}` | Replace the last message and send it again |
| `retry` | | Send the last message again |
| `regenerate` | | Replace the last answer |
| `respond_permission` | `{"id": "perm:…", "reply": "once"}` | Answer a permission prompt: `once`, `always`, `always_persist` or `reject` |
| `answer_question` | `{"id": "ask:…", "reply": {"answered": ["postgres"]}}` | Answer a question, or `{"reply": "cancelled"}` |
| `set_permission_auto_approve` | `true` | Approve every prompt for the rest of the session. Deny rules still apply. |
| `select_model` | `{"provider": "anthropic", "model": "claude-sonnet-5"}` | Switch models |
| `set_thinking_level` | `"high"` | `off`, `minimal`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` or `ultra` |
| `set_mode` | `"plan"` | `build` or `plan`; see [Plan, then build](agent.md#plan-then-build). A name that is not a mode is answered by a `notice`. |
| `request_review` | `{"focus": "error handling"}`, or nothing | A [second opinion](agent.md#a-second-opinion) on the uncommitted changes; answered by `review_started`, then `review_finished` |
| `new_session` | | Start a new session |
| `load_session` | `"<session id>"` | Resume a session; answered by `session_loaded` |
| `refresh_sessions` | | Answered by `sessions_refreshed` |
| `refresh_workspace` | | Answered by `workspace_updated` |
| `request_context_composition` | | What fills the context window; answered by `context_composition` |
| `compact_now` | `{"focus": "the API decisions"}`, or nothing | Summarize now; answered by `compaction_done` |
| `load_guided_review` | `{"request_id": "…", "target": {"kind": "working_tree"}}` | Capture a Guided Review; see [below](#guided-review) |
| `load_file_diff` | `{"request_id": "…", "path": "src/main.rs"}` | One file's change, outside any review; answered by `file_diff_loaded` |
| `list_directory` | `{"request_id": "…", "path": "src"}` | One project folder's entries, without what `.gitignore` ignores unless `"include_ignored": true`, which marks each such entry `"ignored": true`; answered by `directory_listed` |
| `read_project_file` | `{"request_id": "…", "path": "src/main.rs"}` | One project file's text, up to 2 MB; answered by `project_file_read` |
| `close` | | Shut down, stopping a turn in flight the way `cancel` does. The stream ends after it. |

### Guided Review

A review is loaded with `load_guided_review`. Luxe answers with `guided_review_loaded`, which
carries the whole review (its `id`, `revision_id`, files, hunks and chapters), and then always
`review_session_restored`, which carries its comments. Everything below names the review by its
`id`. An action for a review that is no longer the open one is refused.

```text
←  {"kind":"load_guided_review","content":{"request_id":"r1","target":{"kind":"working_tree"}}}
→  {"kind":"guided_review_loaded","content":{"request_id":"r1","review":{"id":"review:…","revision_id":"…",…}}}
→  {"kind":"review_session_restored","content":{"session":{"id":"review:…","findings":[],…}}}
←  {"kind":"edit_review","content":{"request_id":"e1","review_id":"review:…","edit":"comment","anchor":{"kind":"line","file_id":"file:…","hunk_id":"hunk:…","side":"new","line":12},"body":"Why retry twice?","severity":"question","send":true}}
→  {"kind":"review_session_saved","content":{"request_id":"e1","session":{…}}}
```

`edit_review` changes the comments. Every one is answered once, under its `request_id`: with
`review_session_saved` and the stored comments, or `review_session_save_failed` and why. The change
goes in `edit`, beside `request_id` and `review_id`:

| `edit` | Fields | Does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `comment` | `anchor`, `body`; optionally `severity` (`issue` or `question`), `title`, `proposed_fix`, `send` | A new comment. `anchor` is `{"kind":"line","file_id","hunk_id","side","line"}`, a `hunk`, a `chapter`, or `{"kind":"review"}`. The title defaults to the first line. |
| `reply` | `finding_id`, `body`, optionally `send` | A reply on its thread. A resolved comment opens again. |
| `ask_for_fix` | `finding_id`, `body`, optionally `send` | Turn an answered question into a request for the fix |
| `edit_comment` | `finding_id`, `severity`, `title`, `body`, optionally `proposed_fix` | Rewrite a comment not sent yet |
| `delete_comment` | `finding_id` | Delete a comment not sent yet |
| `resolve`, `reopen` | `finding_id` | Mark a comment resolved, or open it again |
| `reanchor` | `finding_id`, `anchor` | Move a comment whose code a refresh moved away |
| `set_outcome` | `outcome`: `accepted`, `changes_requested` or `commented` | Record how the review ended. The agent is not told. |
| `send` | `finding_ids`; optionally `mode` (`request_fixes`, `comment_only`, `question`), `outcome` | Send comments to the agent at the next turn. The mode defaults to what the strongest comment asks for. |
| `cancel_send`, `retry_send` | `submission_id` | Withdraw a send the agent has not started, or send a failed one again |

`send` on a comment, reply or fix request sends it in the same save. A sent comment's turn shows up
as `review_session_saved` while it runs: the agent's answer to a question, and its report on a fix,
are recorded on the comments. You can keep editing while it works.

Each comment's `thread` says who said what, by `author`: `reviewer`, `agent`, or `system` for Luxe's
own word. A fix turn that ends with no report on a comment leaves a `system` entry saying why, and
the comment stays `open`.

| `kind` | `content` | Does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `edit_review` | `{"request_id", "review_id", "edit", …}` | Change the comments, as above |
| `record_review_progress` | `{"review_id", "walked_chapter_ids": [...]}` | Which chapters were read. Saved when it changed, never answered. |
| `record_review_seen` | `{"review_id"}` | Remember what the walked chapters covered, so the next review of the same target leads with what is new |
| `refresh_guided_review` | `{"request_id", "review_id", "revision_id"}` | Read the change again, keeping the comments, if the review is still at `revision_id`. Answered like a load. |
| `commit_review_chapters` | `{"request_id", "review_id", "revision_id", "chapter_ids", "squash"}` | A commit per chapter, or one with `squash`. All chapters when `chapter_ids` is left out. Never pushes. Answered by `review_committed`. |
| `prepare_pull_request` | `{"request_id", "review_id"}` | Draft the pull request this branch's review would open; answered by `pull_request_prepared` |
| `open_pull_request` | `{"request_id", "title", "body", "draft"}` | Open the draft `request_id` named, with your title and description. Commits the reviewed work first when the draft said so. **A GitHub write.** |
| `prepare_stack` | `{"request_id", "review_id"}` | Draft a pull request per chapter; answered by `stack_prepared` |
| `open_stack` | `{"request_id", "draft"}` | Open the drafted stack, bottom first. **A GitHub write.** |
| `prepare_pull_request_post` | `{"request_id", "review_id"}` | Read what posting your review of a pull request needs; answered by `pull_request_post_prepared` |
| `post_pull_request_review` | `{"request_id", "verdict", "session_revision"}` | Post it with `comment`, `approve` or `request_changes`. **A GitHub write.** |
| `prepare_thread_answers` | `{"request_id", "review_id"}` | Whether your fixes are pushed yet, on your own pull request; answered by `thread_answers_prepared` |
| `answer_threads` | `{"request_id", "review_id", "answers": [{"finding_id", "reply", "resolve"}]}` | Reply to and resolve its threads, each named by the comment it became. **A GitHub write.** |

The `open_*` and `post_*` actions confirm a preview by its `request_id`. Luxe keeps what it
prepared, so you send back only what a person can change: a title, a description, a verdict.
`post_pull_request_review` is refused if the comments changed after the `session_revision` you drew
the preview from, so what posts is what you showed. A failed open or post can be confirmed again;
a stack opens once.

### GitHub

These go through your own `gh`, as the interface's `/github` and `/pr` do. `repository` is
`owner/name`, and you leave it out for the checkout's own repository.

| `kind` | `content` | Does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `list_github` | `{"sections": [{"name": "Mine", "query": "is:open is:pr author:@me repo:{repo}"}]}`, or nothing | Run `/github`'s searches. With no `sections`, runs the ones in your config. Answered by `github_listed`. |
| `search_github` | `{"request": 7, "section": {…}, "after": "<cursor>"}` | One search on its own, or its next page; answered by `github_searched` with your `request` |
| `read_github_overview` | `{"repository": "acme/app", "number": 142, "pull_request": true}` | A pull request's or issue's status; answered by `github_overview_read` |
| `read_github_conversation` | `{"number": 142, "pull_request": true}` | Everything said on it; answered by `github_conversation_read` |
| `draft_github_reply` | `{"request_id": "…", "number": 142, "pull_request": true, "target": {…}, "conversation": […]}` | The agent drafts a reply in a turn that changes nothing; answered by `github_reply_drafted`. `target` and `conversation` are what `github_conversation_read` gave you. |
| `check_pull_request_fix` | `{"number": 142}` | Whether it can be checked out here to fix; answered by `pull_request_fix_checked` |
| `plan_restack` | `{"request_id": "restack:…"}` | What restacking this branch's stack would do; answered by `restack_planned`. Luxe keeps the plan. |
| `check_worktree_removal` | | What the session's worktree has not committed; answered by `worktree_removal_checked` |
| `set_focus` | `{"focused": false}` | Whether your window has focus. Luxe checks GitHub less often while it does not. |
| `link_pull_request` | `{"number": 142, "url": "…"}` | Record that this session worked on that pull request |
| `post_github_comment` | `{"number": 142, "thread": "PRRT_…", "body": "Fixed."}` | Post a reply in a thread, or a comment without `thread`; answered by `github_comment_posted`. **A GitHub write.** |
| `change_pull_request` | `{"number": 142, "write": {"change": "mark_ready"}}` | `update_branch`, `mark_ready`, `merge`, `enable_auto_merge` or `disable_auto_merge`; answered by `pull_request_changed`. **A GitHub write.** |
| `restack` | `{"request_id": "restack:…"}` | Push the plan `plan_restack` made under that id, exactly as planned; answered by `restacked` or `restack_failed`. **A GitHub write.** |

You confirm a restack by its id, not by sending the plan back: Luxe pushes the plan it showed you. A
newer `plan_restack` replaces the older plan, and a plan is pushed once. Before pushing, Luxe checks
that every moving branch here is where the plan saw it, checked out where it was, and clean, and
refuses with `restack_failed` otherwise. A push that did not finish is also `restack_failed`, and
its message says to check the branches on GitHub, since some may have moved. If the push succeeds
but the branches here, or a pull request's base on GitHub, cannot follow, the answer is `restacked`,
with what went wrong in `retarget_failed`. A `restack_planned` with nothing to restack, such as no
open pull request or no `gh`, carries a `refusal` and no `plan`.

`--issue`, `--from-pr` and `--worktree` work with `--rpc` as they do anywhere, since they decide the
session before the first frame. See [Git and GitHub](github.md).

An unknown `kind` is answered with `action_rejected`, which is also how to find out what a build
supports. So is a malformed line, and nothing else happens: one bad line never ends the session.

```text
←  {"kind":"steer_turn","content":{}}
→  {"kind":"action_rejected","content":{"kind":"steer_turn","reason":"steer_turn: missing field `text`"}}
```

## Events

There are around sixty. These are the ones a front end is built on:

| `kind` | Is |
| --- | --- |
| `ready` | The handshake: protocol version, Luxe version, session ID, directory |
| `token_delta`, `thinking_delta` | The reply and reasoning as they stream. `block` orders them. |
| `tool_call_composing` | The model has started writing a tool call. Optional; useful for showing a `write` filling in. |
| `tool_started`, `tool_progress`, `tool_completed`, `tool_ended` | A tool call's progress, by `call_id`. `tool_completed` carries its output. |
| `tool_activity_updated` | The card the interface draws for a call: title, body, state and timing |
| `message_committed` | A complete message was added to the transcript |
| `permission_requested` | **Answer it** with `respond_permission`, or the turn waits. If `always_patterns` is empty, offer only `once` and `reject`. |
| `question_asked` | **Answer it** with `answer_question` |
| `turn_ended` | The turn finished; `reason` says why |
| `provider_retrying` | The provider failed before answering, and Luxe is trying again |
| `state_changed` | Model, thinking level, mode, and whether a turn is running |
| `plan_written` | Plan mode wrote `path`. The interface offers the plan's next step when the turn ends. |
| `review_started`, `review_finished` | A requested review began on `model`, and came back with a `verdict` (`continue`, `fix` or `unavailable`) and `findings`. On `fix` the findings also become the agent's next turn. |
| `turn_usage`, `session_usage`, `plan_usage` | Cost per call, for the session, and what a subscription has left |
| `context_usage`, `context_composition` | How full the context window is, and with what |
| `workspace_updated` | The project, Git changes, todos and tools: what the dock shows |
| `session_loaded`, `sessions_refreshed` | A transcript was restored; the session list changed |
| `notice`, `error` | Something to show. `error` ends the turn. |
| `action_rejected` | Your frame was refused and nothing happened |

Guided Review, as the interface sees it:

| `kind` | Is |
| --- | --- |
| `guided_review_loading`, `guided_review_loaded`, `guided_review_failed` | A review you asked for, by `request_id`. `loaded` carries the whole review: files, hunks and chapters. |
| `guided_review_guide_updated` | Better chapters and a summary replaced the first ones, for the same pinned revision |
| `review_session_restored` | The comments and progress that go with the review just loaded. It always follows `guided_review_loaded`, after a restart too. |
| `review_session_saved`, `review_session_save_failed` | A change to them was stored, or refused. Luxe reports its own changes this way too: a turn starting, the agent's report, a review posted. |
| `review_feedback_turn_dispatched`, `review_feedback_turn_completed`, `review_feedback_turn_failed` | Feedback you sent reaching the agent, and how its turn went |
| `review_questions_answered`, `remediation_reported` | The agent's answer to a question, and its report on a fix |
| `review_committed`, `review_commit_failed` | Committing a review's chapters |
| `last_turn_available` | The agent's last turn can be reviewed on its own |
| `file_diff_loaded`, `file_diff_failed` | One file's change, for `load_file_diff` |
| `directory_listed`, `directory_list_failed` | One folder's entries, for `list_directory` |
| `project_file_read`, `project_file_read_failed` | One file's text, for `read_project_file` |

GitHub:

| `kind` | Is |
| --- | --- |
| `github_listed`, `github_searched` | Search results, with each section's rows or why it has none |
| `github_overview_read`, `github_conversation_read` | One pull request or issue: its status, or everything said on it |
| `github_reply_drafted`, `github_comment_posted` | A draft to edit and send, and where a sent one was posted |
| `pull_request_changed`, `pull_request_fix_checked` | What a change did, and whether a fix can be checked out here |
| `restack_planned`, `restacked`, `restack_failed` | A restack's plan, and what pushing it did |
| `pull_request_prepared`, `pull_request_opened`, `pull_request_open_failed` | Opening a pull request from a review |
| `stack_prepared`, `stack_opened` | Opening a review as a stack |
| `pull_request_post_prepared`, `pull_request_review_posted`, `pull_request_post_failed` | Posting your review of a pull request |
| `thread_answers_prepared`, `threads_answered`, `thread_answers_failed` | Replying to and resolving review threads on your own pull request |
| `worktree_removal_checked` | What removing the session's worktree would lose |

The branch's pull request, its checks and its review status come in `workspace_updated`, as they
do for the interface's dock.

Treat an event you do not recognize as nothing.

## Versioning

`protocol_version` is `2`. New events, actions and fields do not change it, since a client that
ignores what it does not know already handles them. It changes only when something a client could
have relied on is removed or renamed. So dispatch on `kind`, ignore the rest, and do not assume the
list is closed.

## Security

- Luxe listens on nothing; your client is the process that started it.
- Permission rules are enforced inside Luxe. A client cannot weaken a `deny`: reading `.env` is
  refused here as everywhere.
- Prompts go to your client to answer. To approve everything, send `set_permission_auto_approve` or
  start with `--auto-approve`. `--on-ask` is refused, since your client can answer.
- `--permission-mode`, `--read-only`, `--yolo` and `--trust-project` apply as usual.

### GitHub writes

Your client can read GitHub without asking. To let it publish there (post a comment or a review,
answer threads, open, change, merge or restack a pull request), start Luxe with `--github-writes`.
Without it, those actions are refused with `action_rejected`, and `ready` says
`"github_writes": false` so you can hide them.

- **Read-only wins.** With `--read-only`, or a read-only mode in your permissions file, the writes
  are refused even with the flag, and so is `commit_review_chapters`.
- **It is a flag, not a setting.** Whoever starts Luxe decides, for that session. No config file
  turns it on, and a project cannot.
- **It covers your client, not the agent.** The agent's own GitHub writes are permission rules: they
  ask first, and the prompt comes to your client. See [Security](security.md#when-you-step-away).

Luxe is not a sandbox. To isolate it, run it in a [container](security.md#isolation).
@@@ page: security
---
title: "Security and permissions"
summary: "What the agent may do, the rules and prompts that decide it, secrets, and what Luxe sends over the network."
order: 1
group: "Reference"
---

The agent reads and writes files and runs commands on your machine. Luxe lets ordinary work through
without asking, keeps a few guardrails on at all times, and gives you rules to tighten the rest.
For real isolation, run it in a [container](#isolation).

## What is allowed by default

Every tool call is **allowed**, **asked** about, or **denied**. With no configuration:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Denied** | Reading `.env` and `.env.*` files (`.env.example` is fine). Catastrophic commands: wiping `/`, your home folder or a system folder, `mkfs`, `dd` to a device, fork bombs. Running a command as root; see [below](#commands-that-need-root). The same call with the same arguments a third time in a row: the agent is told it already has the result. |
| **Asked** | Anything outside the project folder. `git push --force`. Committing. Writes to GitHub: opening, merging or commenting on pull requests and issues, and re-running CI. Capturing your screen. |
| **Allowed** | Everything else |

Commands are matched piece by piece, so `cd /tmp && rm -rf /` is caught. These are guardrails, not
a security boundary: a model set on getting around a pattern can. Committing asks because a commit
moves what Guided Review compares against; answer **Allow always** once and it stops asking.

Recursive `rm` has its own check, covering `-r`, `-R`, combined flags, `--recursive` and an
end-of-options `--`. It catches `/`, `/*`, whole-home targets such as `~`, `$HOME` and `${HOME}`,
and protected system folders and their contents. Ordinary build-folder cleanup stays allowed.
`/etc-backup/` isn't `/etc`, so its name alone doesn't trigger this guard.
A Bash allowance or session approval cannot waive this check; `--yolo` disables the default guard.

## Permission modes

```bash
luxe --permission-mode strict
```

| Mode | |
| --- | --- |
| `default` | The defaults above |
| `strict` | Ask before every change: `write`, `edit`, `bash`, `git`, `debug`, a `test` with its own `command`, and an applied `ast_grep` or `lsp_navigation` change |
| `read-only` | Deny every change, and a `test` with its own `command`. Reading, search, code intelligence and detected tests still work. Also `--read-only`. |
| `yolo` | Allow everything, guardrails off. Also `--yolo`. Your own `deny` rules still apply. |

[Plan mode](agent.md#plan-then-build) is a different thing: the session's mode, not a permission
mode. It refuses every change but a write to the plan file, before the permission rules are asked,
so a rule that allows a command does not let plan mode run it. A [review](agent.md#a-second-opinion)
runs in a mode that refuses every change.

## Rules

```json title="~/.config/luxe/permissions.json"
{
  "mode": "default",
  "permission": {
    "bash": { "*": "allow", "rm *": "ask", "git push * --force *": "deny" },
    "git": { "commit*": "allow" },
    "read": { "*": "allow", "*.env": "deny", "*.env.example": "allow" },
    "external_directory": { "~/scratch/**": "allow" },
    "mcp": { "github/*": "ask" }
  }
}
```

- **Keys** are tool names (`bash`, `read`, `edit`, which also covers `write`, `glob`, `grep`, `git`,
  `webfetch`, `websearch`, `screenshot`, `mcp`), plus `external_directory` for paths outside the
  project, `doom_loop` for repeated calls, and `hook_ask` for [hooks](hooks.md) that ask.
- **Values** are `allow`, `ask` or `deny`, or a map from pattern to one of them.
- **Patterns**: `*` matches anything, `?` one character, and `~` your home folder. `git *` also
  matches `git` alone. A `bash` pattern matches the command; a `read` or `edit` pattern, the path;
  an `mcp` pattern, `server/tool`.
- **The most specific pattern wins.**

Bash chains are also checked segment by segment. An allowance for `git *` does not allow
`git status && curl example.com`: the `curl` segment needs its own allowance. A denied segment
blocks the call. Otherwise, if any segment asks, the call asks too. Every segment must be allowed
for the whole chain to run without asking. The matcher is best-effort, not a shell parser.

Tools that run a program, change files or search a folder are judged by the same rules:

| Tool | Also checked as |
| --- | --- |
| `test` with a `command` | `bash`, segment by segment, with its `filter`; a filter that hides a second command is checked too |
| `debug` `launch` | `bash`, as the program and its arguments; a shell's `-c` script is checked as a command of its own |
| `ast_grep` replace with `apply: true` | `edit`, for each path |
| `lsp_navigation` rename or code action with `apply: true` | `edit`, for the file |
| `grep`, `glob`, `ast_grep` | `read`, for the folder or file searched |
| `module_report`, `read_symbol`, `lsp_navigation`, `lsp_diagnostics` | `read`, for each file opened |

Each tool's own rules still apply alongside. A folder outside the project asks, and a named `.env`
is denied even with `all: true`. **Always** on these prompts remembers only what was asked: the
exact command for `test` and `debug`, the folder for one search outside the project, and nothing
for an applied change, since its files aren't known until it runs.

`grep` and `ast_grep` also check every file they find before reading it, so a search of the whole
project skips a nested `.env`; `glob` checks every name before listing it. A file your rules deny is
skipped. One that would ask is read when the run approves asks on its own (headless by default, or
with auto-approve on) and skipped otherwise, since a search can't stop to ask. The result says how
many were skipped; `read` the file to be asked. A walk over a huge tree stops at 100,000 files and
says so.

An applied rename or code action is refused whole if the language server's edit names a file
outside the project or inside a fetched repository. These checks cover what a tool is asked to
open. They don't sandbox a language server, which can index other files and runs the project's own
code.

A project's `.luxe/permissions.json` can only make your rules stricter, never looser, unless you
start Luxe with `--trust-project`.

## The permission prompt

When a call needs approval, a prompt opens above the composer:

![A commit waiting for approval, offering to remember git commit*](images/security-permission-prompt.svg)

| Choice | Does |
| --- | --- |
| **Allow once** | Run this call |
| **Allow for this session** | Allow calls like it until you quit |
| **Allow always** | Write the rule to your `~/.config/luxe/permissions.json` |
| **Reject** | Refuse; the agent is told and carries on |

The prompt shows the rule an **Allow always** would write: a command family, such as `cargo *`, or
the whole folder for a path outside the project. A hook's prompt or a chained Bash command offers
only **Allow once** and **Reject**: one command family cannot cover a chain. Choose with the
arrows and `enter`, or a number; `esc` rejects. For a moment after it opens, the prompt ignores
every key but `esc`, so typing meant for the composer cannot answer it.

## When you step away

**Auto-approve** (`/permissions on`, or `--auto-approve`) allows every call that would ask, while
your `deny` rules still hold. The statusline says `auto-approve` for as long as it is on.

**A run with nobody to answer**, such as `--headless`, `luxe loop` or a phase reviewer, allows
every `ask` by default. To refuse them instead, and tell the agent why:

```bash
luxe --headless --on-ask deny -p "…"
```

or `"agent": { "on_ask": "deny" }` in `config.json`. A project can set `deny` but not `allow`.

**Four GitHub actions need a person**: merging a pull request, closing one, submitting a review, and
closing an issue. Auto-approve and unattended runs refuse them. To let an unattended run do one,
allow it in your own rules, such as `"bash": { "gh pr merge *": "allow" }`.

## Secrets

- Credentials are stored in `~/.config/luxe/auth.json`, readable only by you. Luxe warns if
  `auth.json` or `models.json` can be read by others.
- A key is found in this order: `--api-key` or `LUXE_API_KEY`, then what you signed in with, then
  the provider's own variable, then a provider block in `auth.json` or `models.json`. For a provider
  Luxe does not know, the block comes before `OPENAI_API_KEY`. The order is the same for the
  provider a session starts on and for one you switch to in `/model`.
- A key can be `$VAR` or `!command` rather than the value, so it never sits in a file. A command
  runs when a key is needed, so treat these files like your shell's startup file. It runs from your
  home folder and is stopped after 30 seconds, so a password manager that asks for a passphrase
  needs a graphical prompt.
- Anything that looks like a secret (API keys, tokens, private keys, passwords in URLs) is removed
  from tool output before the model, the transcript, hooks or the log see it. So is every key and
  token Luxe itself has used or loaded, whatever it looks like, including `$VAR` and `!command`
  keys and MCP tokens, as long as it is at least 8 characters.
- MCP sign-in tokens are kept in `~/.local/state/luxe/mcp-auth.json`, outside your config folder,
  so a dotfiles repository never carries them.
- An MCP server's `auth` token or OAuth sign-in only travels over `https`, or plain `http` to
  this machine; a server or sign-in endpoint elsewhere on plain `http` is refused. A key you put in
  a server's `headers` is not checked, so use `https` for one. See [MCP](mcp.md#sign-in).
- Anthropic and Google take API keys only, since their terms do not allow their subscriptions in
  other programs.

## Commands that need root

The agent does not run commands as root: `sudo`, `doas`, `su`, `pkexec`, `run0`, and `gsudo` or
`runas` on Windows. A command that needs root needs your attention and consent, and typing it into
your own terminal is how you give both. So when a step needs one, the agent puts the exact command
in a code block, you copy it into another terminal and run it, then tell the agent it is done.

The same goes for a command that waits on you at a terminal, such as a password, a confirmation or
an interactive installer. Commands the agent runs have no terminal at all, so one of those fails at
once and says what it wanted, rather than waiting where nobody can answer.

To allow it anyway, decide ahead of time in your global file. It only helps where no password is
needed, such as a passwordless `sudo` rule for one program:

```json title="~/.config/luxe/permissions.json"
{ "permission": { "bash": { "sudo pacman *": "allow" } } }
```

`--yolo` allows it too. A project's `.luxe/permissions.json` cannot.

## Screen capture

The `screenshot` tool's `url` mode renders a web page and captures only that. Its `fullscreen`,
`region` and `window` modes capture whatever is on your screen, and the image goes to your model
provider, so each **asks** first, and runs with nobody watching refuse them. To turn screen capture
off entirely:

```json title="~/.config/luxe/permissions.json"
{ "permission": { "screenshot": { "fullscreen": "deny", "region": "deny", "window": "deny" } } }
```

## Untrusted repositories

Opening a repository should not run its code. So, without `--trust-project`:

- Its `.luxe/hooks.json` is ignored.
- Its `gate.commands` in `.luxe/config.json` are ignored with a warning. The loop uses your global
  commands instead; a project list needs `--trust-project`.
- Its `.luxe/permissions.json` can only tighten your rules.
- Its MCP servers, language servers and formatters start only in an interactive session; see
  [Tools](tools.md#a-server-the-project-installed).

Its `AGENTS.md` and skills, including the ones it commits in `.agents/skills/`, still reach the
model, because your own project's are the point of the feature. Luxe removes text a reviewer
cannot see, comments and invisible Unicode, and leaves out a file it cannot finish checking; see
[What Luxe removes](project-context.md#what-luxe-removes). Plain text is still instructions, so read
an unfamiliar repository's `AGENTS.md` as you would its `Makefile`.
Text from GitHub, such as issues and comments, is filtered the same way and given to the agent as
someone else's words, not as instructions. So are MCP servers' descriptions and results.

A language server can run project code itself: rust-analyzer runs `build.rs`. Treat opening a
repository in Luxe like building it.

A repository the agent fetches with `web_fetch` is different: you never chose to open it. Luxe
clones it into `.luxe/gh-cache/` with symbolic links flattened to plain files, and starts no
language server or formatter there; see [Tools](tools.md#github-repositories).

### Isolation

Rules are a policy, not a sandbox. For hard isolation, run Luxe in a container that mounts only the
project:

```bash
docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD":/work -w /work -e ANTHROPIC_API_KEY <image-with-luxe> \
  luxe --headless -p "…"
```

Do not mount your home folder or SSH keys. `--network none` works for everything but the model
provider, the web tools, the catalog refresh and the update check.

## What Luxe sends over the network

There is no telemetry. Luxe connects only to:

1. The model provider you configured, including the cache refreshes described in
   [Keeping the cache warm](sessions.md#keeping-the-cache-warm) (`"agent": { "cache_warming": "off" }`
   stops them). For GitHub Copilot that includes reading your plan's usage from GitHub every few
   minutes while you work (`LUXE_COPILOT_PLAN_USAGE=0` stops it). For an Azure resource it includes
   listing what the resource has deployed when you open `/model` (`"discover_deployments": false`
   on the provider stops it)
2. Search providers and web pages, when the agent uses `web_search` or `web_fetch`, and GitHub
   when `web_fetch` clones a repository (`"tools": { "clone_repositories": false }` stops it)
3. The models.dev catalog, to refresh model details (`LUXE_MODELS_DEV_REFRESH=0` stops it)
4. The update check, once a day (`"update": { "check": false }` stops it), and when you run
   `luxe update` or `/update`, which then runs your package manager's own update
5. GitHub, through your own `gh`, when you, the agent or an [RPC client](rpc.md#github-writes) work
   with pull requests and issues. A client can write there only if you start it with
   `--github-writes`.

None of them carries anything about you or your machine. The update check sends no version,
platform or identifier; it downloads a public file and compares versions locally.

One local report stays on your machine: inside a [herdr](configuration.md#herdr) pane, Luxe runs
herdr's own command to tell it whether the agent is working, idle or waiting on you, and the id of
the session for herdr to resume. Nothing is sent outside herdr, and `"herdr": false` stops it.

What you post to GitHub is yours alone: reviews, replies and pull requests are posted from a
preview, with nothing added, and no agent tool can post them.

## Supply chain

Luxe is written in Rust with `unsafe` code denied throughout, apart from two reviewed blocks in what
ships: one starts each command in a session of its own, so nothing the agent runs can reach your
terminal, and one on Windows keeps the programs Luxe starts off the stdin `--rpc` reads. CI checks
every dependency's security advisories and license with `cargo-deny`, builds with `--locked`, and
pins its GitHub Actions to exact commits.
@@@ page: sessions
---
title: "Sessions and context"
summary: "Resume past sessions, see what fills the context window, and how Luxe keeps long sessions going."
order: 8
group: "Using Luxe"
---

## Sessions

Every conversation is saved as it goes, in `.luxe/sessions/` inside the project. Quitting loses
nothing.

| To | In Luxe | From the command line |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pick up the last session | **Resume** on the start screen | `luxe -c` |
| Find an older one | Type part of its title on the start screen, or open **Sessions…** (`/sessions`) | `luxe sessions list`, then `luxe --resume <id>` |
| Return to the session that worked on a pull request | type `#146` in **Sessions…** | `luxe --from-pr 146` |
| Start fresh | `/new`, or type on the start screen and press `enter` | `luxe` |

![Sessions…, with the selected session's conversation previewed](images/sessions-picker.svg)

**Sessions…** searches session titles and what was said in them, with a preview of the one under
the cursor. `/sessions` opens it from the start screen or from inside a session. However you resume a
session, it runs in its own worktree when it has one, and keeps what you had typed and the mode,
model and thinking level you chose. `/new` keeps the session you leave, so you can come back to it.

## Cost

The dock's **SESSION** section shows context used, tokens and cost as you go. `/cost` shows the
session's cost with the tokens behind it, how much of the input was read from the provider's cache,
and, once more than one of them has spent something, the split between `agent`, `review`,
`compaction` and `cache warming`. On a ChatGPT or
Copilot plan, it shows what the usage would have cost at API prices, and what is left of the plan's
allowance when the provider reports it. A model that charges more for a long prompt, as models.dev
lists for some Claude and Gemini models, is priced at the higher rate for each request past the
threshold. A price you set in `models.json` replaces the catalog's, tiers and all.

### Keeping the cache warm

Anthropic keeps a cached prompt for five minutes after it was last read. A turn that waits longer
than that, on a slow command, a permission prompt or a question, loses the cache, and the next
request pays to write the whole conversation again: about $2 on a 400k-token Opus session. So while
a turn runs, Luxe re-sends its last request with a one-token reply just before the five minutes are
up. That costs a cache read, a tenth of the write it saves.

`agent.cache_warming` decides when:

| Value | Keeps the cache warm |
| --- | --- |
| `streaming` (default) | While a turn is running |
| `idle` | While a turn is running, and for up to 30 minutes after it |
| `off` | Never |

A refresh goes out only when it is expected to save at least $0.05, so a short conversation is
never refreshed. Between turns Luxe cannot know you will reply, so `idle` refreshes only a large
conversation. On real sessions it lost money overall, which is why it is not the default. Refreshes
are never sent on a subscription plan, or for an Anthropic model using a fixed thinking budget,
whose cache would change on replay. Their cost shows under **cache warming** in `/cost`.

The other answer to a long pause is `supports_long_cache_retention`, which asks Anthropic to keep
the cache for an hour; see [Custom providers](custom-providers.md#request-format). It costs
more on every turn instead of on each pause.

## The context window

`/context` shows what fills the context window, largest first:

```text
 GPT-5.6 Sol   18.5k of 1.1M · 2% used

  conversation     9.6k   52%
      `read` crat…-tui/src/statusline.rs   9.2k
  tool schemas     4.5k   25%
  instructions     2.8k   15%
  harness          1.5k    8%
  free             1.0M
```

| Row | Is | Shrink it with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| conversation | Messages, tool calls and results, reasoning, images | `/compact`, `/new` |
| tool schemas | The tools the agent can call | `tools.disabled`; see [Tools](tools.md) |
| instructions | Your `AGENTS.md` files | A shorter file; see [Project context](project-context.md) |
| skills | The list of skills the agent can load | Fewer, or shorter descriptions |
| harness | Luxe's own instructions | Nothing; this is fixed |
| appended | One-time context added to a resumed session, such as what changed while you were away | `/new` |

The largest single items are named under a row, which is usually how you find a `read` or `bash`
call that should have been narrower. The total is what the provider reported for the last request.

## Compaction

When a conversation fills 90% of the usable window, Luxe summarizes it and carries on, keeping the
most recent part word for word. The summary records the goal, constraints, progress, decisions,
next steps and the files the session touched. You see a line like
`Compacted the conversation — 82k → 21k of context.`

`/compact` summarizes now. Add what matters to steer the summary: `/compact the API decisions`. A
conversation that already fits in what `keep_recent` keeps has nothing to summarize, and `/compact`
says so.

Before summarizing, from 80% full, Luxe first replaces old tool output in the request with a short
placeholder. The session file keeps everything; only what is sent changes.

To change when and how it happens:

```json title="~/.config/luxe/config.json"
{
  "compaction": {
    "auto": true,
    "at": 0.9,
    "keep_recent": 20000,
    "reserve": 20000,
    "prune": true,
    "summarizer": "anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5"
  }
}
```

| Key | Default | Does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `auto` | `true` | Summarize automatically. Off leaves it to `/compact` and turns pruning off too; a request the provider refuses as too long is still summarized and sent again, once. |
| `at` | `0.9` | How full the usable window gets before summarizing. Pruning starts 0.1 earlier. |
| `keep_recent` | `20000` | Tokens of the newest conversation kept word for word |
| `reserve` | `20000` | Most tokens held back for the reply when judging how full the window is, or the model's output limit if that is smaller |
| `prune` | `true` | Replace old tool output before summarizing |
| `summarizer` | the session's model | The model that writes the summary, as `provider/id`, on a provider you have set up. A smaller, cheaper model is usually enough, and `/cost` prices its spend as it does any other model's. |

This works in a project's `.luxe/config.json` too, and so does `agent.cache_warming`, which a project
can turn down but not up. The compaction settings in `/settings` apply the next time Luxe starts.

## Long command output

Build, test and lint output is trimmed before the agent sees it. Errors, warnings, failing tests,
`file:line` locations and exit codes are always kept; progress bars, color codes and repeated lines
are not. When output is trimmed, the untouched text is saved under `.luxe/artifacts/` (each stream
whole up to 8 MB, or its first and last 4 MB past that) and its path is included, so the agent can
read it if it needs to. Set `LUXE_COMPRESS=0` to turn this off; output past the size limit is still
cut and saved.

Searches and listings (`grep`, `glob`, `git log`) are capped the same way, with a note saying how
many more results there are.
@@@ page: skills
---
title: "Skills"
summary: "Teach the agent a procedure it loads only when it needs it."
order: 2
group: "Extend"
---

A skill is a playbook in a `SKILL.md` file: how your team reviews a migration, cuts a release or
writes a changelog entry. The agent sees each skill's name and description, and loads the full text
only when a task calls for it, so a long skill costs nothing until it is used.

## Write a skill

One folder per skill, with a `SKILL.md` in it:

| Folder | For |
| --- | --- |
| `~/.agents/skills/<name>/` | Every project, and every agent that reads it |
| `~/.config/luxe/skills/<name>/` | Every project (`%APPDATA%\luxe\skills` on Windows) |
| `.agents/skills/<name>/` | This repository, committed with it |
| `.luxe/skills/<name>/` | This project. Git sees it too, since `.luxe/` keeps `skills/` out of what it ignores. |

`.agents/skills/` is where Codex, OpenCode, Pi, GitHub Copilot and the `npx skills` installer put
skills, so one installed for any of them works here too. Luxe reads a repository's `.agents/skills/`
from the top of the repository down to the project. When two skills share a name, whatever its case,
the one lower in the table wins, so a project's skill replaces your own, and between nested
`.agents/skills/` folders the deeper one wins. A skill reached twice through a symbolic link counts
once.

```markdown title=".luxe/skills/release-notes/SKILL.md"
---
name: release-notes
description: >
  Writes the CHANGELOG entry for a user-visible change. Use when a change
  adds, removes or alters something a user would notice.
---

1. Read the diff and the issue it closes.
2. Add one line under `## Unreleased` in CHANGELOG.md, in the past tense,
   naming what changed for the user, not how.
3. Link the pull request at the end of the line.
```

Write the description for the moment the agent decides whether to load it: say when to use it, not
what it contains. Without one, the agent sees only the name. `name` is optional and defaults to the
folder's, and the `---` block has to start on the first line.

A skill folder can also hold reference files. A loaded skill tells the agent its folder, so a
skill that says *see `references/schema.md`* gets read. A skill over 40,000 characters is cut off,
with a note telling the agent to read the rest of the file.

## Use a skill

The agent loads a skill when its description fits the task. To ask for one yourself, mention it:
`@`, `tab` to **Skills**, and `enter`, as in *split this into a stack with @[skill:gh-stack]*.

**Project context** lists the skills Luxe found: type `skills` on the start screen and open it. A
`SKILL.md` placed directly in `skills/`, without its own folder, is skipped, and Luxe names it at
startup. The list in the agent's instructions is read with a session's first message, and again
when you resume one. The `@` picker and the `skill` tool look again every time, so a skill added
mid-session can be mentioned or loaded at once.

## Install a skill

Skills written for other agents use the same format and work as they are. Installing one is copying
its folder:

```bash
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/github/gh-stack /tmp/gh-stack
mkdir -p ~/.config/luxe/skills
cp -r /tmp/gh-stack/skills/gh-stack ~/.config/luxe/skills/
```

Create `skills/` first, as above. Without it, `cp -r` copies the skill's contents to `skills/`
itself, one level too high.

A skill's text reaches the model as instructions, so read a skill before installing it, as you
would a script. The same goes for a repository you clone: its `.agents/skills/` and
`.luxe/skills/` reach the model without `--trust-project`. Luxe removes comments and invisible
characters from skill files, as it does from [`AGENTS.md`](project-context.md#what-luxe-removes),
but without a notice.
@@@ page: tools
---
title: "Tools"
summary: "What the agent can use: files, the shell, tests, Git, code intelligence, a debugger and the web."
order: 10
group: "Using Luxe"
---

## What the agent can use

| Tool | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `read` | Read files, several at once, with numbered lines. A long file comes back a page at a time. An image is read as a picture for models that can see. |
| `write`, `edit` | Write or change a file. A file must be read before it is edited, and the card shows the diff, after [formatting](#format-on-save). |
| `bash` | Run a shell command. Long output is trimmed, and the untouched output saved under `.luxe/artifacts/`: each stream whole up to 8 MB, or its first and last 4 MB past that. |
| `test` | Run the project's tests and report each failure with its `file:line`, and which tests your change broke. Output is saved as `bash`'s is. |
| `grep`, `glob` | Search file contents and names, with capped output. `grep` names each file once with its matching lines under it, and can say which function or type each match sits in. |
| `ast_grep` | Search and replace by code structure. Needs [ast-grep](https://ast-grep.github.io). |
| `git` | Status, diffs, history, commits, branches, and GitHub pull requests, issues and CI checks through `gh` |
| `todo` | The agent's checklist, shown in the dock's **PLAN** |
| `question` | Ask you a question with choices, in a picker |
| `skill` | Load a [skill](skills.md) |
| `symbol_search`, `read_symbol`, `module_report` | Find symbols across the project and read one without the whole file |
| `impact` | What else a change to a symbol or file affects: callers, dependents and covering tests |
| `lsp_diagnostics`, `lsp_navigation` | Errors and warnings, definitions, references and types, from a [language server](#code-intelligence) |
| `debug` | Drive a [debugger](#debugger): breakpoints, stepping, inspecting variables. Offered when a debug adapter is installed. |
| `web_search`, `web_fetch` | Search the web and read pages; see [Web](#web) |
| `screenshot` | Capture a web page or your own dev server, with a Chromium-based browser, or with your approval, your screen; see [Screen capture](security.md#screen-capture) |
| `mcp` | Call tools on the [MCP servers](mcp.md) you configured, when there are any |

Each tool has to beat the shell command it replaces. [luxe.dev/tools](https://luxe.dev/tools)
shows how, measured.

A call with an argument the tool does not know still runs, and its result names the argument it
ignored, with the one the agent probably meant.

`/tools` lists what the agent can use in the current session, and why any tool is missing. Some tools are sent with every
request; the rest are listed by name and loaded when the agent first needs one, which keeps every
request smaller.

The `test` tool runs tests the way the project does: through its own `.venv` or the package
manager its lockfile names (`uv`, `poetry`, `pnpm`, `yarn` and so on), not whatever happens to be
on `PATH`.

## Turn tools off

The Tools page of [`/settings`](configuration.md#settings) turns each one on or off, or set it in
the file:

```json title="~/.config/luxe/config.json"
{ "tools": { "disabled": ["web_search", "screenshot"] } }
```

A change applies the next time Luxe starts, since the tools the agent is offered are fixed for a
run.

For one session, `luxe --no-tool web_search` turns a tool off and `luxe --with-tool web_search`
turns one back on. `read`, `write`, `edit` and `bash` cannot be turned off.

## Format on save

Each file the agent writes or edits goes through its formatter, and the result shows the file as
the formatter left it. That includes a file changed by an applied rename, code action or `ast_grep`
rewrite. rustfmt and gofmt always run. The others run only where the project has
their config, in the file's directory or one above it:

| Language | Formatter | Runs when the project has |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rust | rustfmt, at the project's edition | always |
| Go | gofmt | always |
| Python | ruff | `ruff.toml`, `.ruff.toml`, or `[tool.ruff]` in `pyproject.toml` |
| TypeScript, JavaScript | biome | `biome.json` or `biome.jsonc` |
| TOML | taplo | `taplo.toml` or `.taplo.toml` |

A formatter that is not installed is skipped. When Luxe pipes a file through one (taplo), an empty
answer, or a file that changed again while it ran, leaves the file as it was. To turn formatting
off:

```json title="~/.config/luxe/config.json"
{ "tools": { "format_on_save": false } }
```

## Time limits

Every tool call has a time limit, after which it is stopped: 120 seconds, or 60 for tools that wait
on the network. `bash` defaults to 30 seconds and `test` to 300, and the agent can ask for longer,
up to an hour. `question` waits for you as long as it takes. `LUXE_TOOL_TIMEOUT_SECS` replaces the
120- and 60-second limits; `bash` and `test` keep their own.

`ctrl+esc` stops the whole batch of calls, not just the one running. A call that never started is
reported as having had no effect; one stopped partway says so, since it may have done half its work.

A command that starts something and leaves it running, such as a dev server, returns when the
command itself ends. The server keeps running.

Tools work from the directory Luxe was started in. A `cd` inside one `bash` call does not carry over
to the next, so start Luxe in the project you want to work on.

## Code intelligence

After every edit, Luxe asks the file's language server for errors and warnings and adds the ones
the edit introduced to the result the agent sees, so it can fix what it broke before moving on.
Problems that were already in the file are counted, not listed. The result also names changed code
that no test covers. Set `LUXE_LSP_ON_EDIT=0` to turn both off.

The agent is held to small files and functions: 500 lines and 20 lines. When an edit takes a file
or a function past one of those for the first time, the result says so, so the agent can split it
while the change is fresh. A file that was already long says nothing more. Functions are measured
in Rust, Python, Go, TypeScript and JavaScript; files in any language. Set `LUXE_SIZE_CHECK=0` to turn this off, for a project whose own
conventions differ.

Luxe launches these language servers when they are installed:

| Language | Server | Install |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rust | rust-analyzer | `rustup component add rust-analyzer` |
| TypeScript, JavaScript | typescript-language-server, `tsgo` for TypeScript 7, or `tsc --lsp` | `npm i -g typescript-language-server typescript` |
| Python | pyright, or basedpyright | `npm i -g pyright` |
| Go | gopls | `go install golang.org/x/tools/gopls@latest` |
| C, C++ | clangd | `apt install clangd`, `brew install llvm` |
| Bash | bash-language-server | `npm i -g bash-language-server` |
| Ruby | ruby-lsp, or solargraph | `gem install ruby-lsp` |
| Lua | lua-language-server | `mise use -g lua-language-server` |
| Svelte | svelte-language-server | `npm i -g svelte-language-server` |
| JSON | vscode-json-language-server | `npm i -g vscode-langservers-extracted` |
| YAML | yaml-language-server | `npm i -g yaml-language-server` |

A rename or code action the agent applies writes only inside the project. An edit naming a file
anywhere else, or inside a [fetched repository](#github-repositories), is refused whole. Otherwise
every file is written or none is, and the result says which edits didn't fit their file and which
file operations, such as creating or renaming one, it left undone.

`/lsp` shows which servers are running, and `luxe doctor` starts each one to check it works. Luxe
never installs a server itself. When one is missing, the result tells the agent the command that
installs it, which runs through `bash` under your rules like any other.

### A server the project installed

Luxe prefers the copy a project installed for itself, in its `node_modules/.bin` or virtual
environment, since that version matches the project. The same goes for formatters such as `ruff`
and `biome`, and for MCP servers a project declares. Runs with nobody watching, such as
`--headless` and the loop, use only what you installed yourself unless you pass `--trust-project`.
To decide for every run, in your own config:

```json title="~/.config/luxe/config.json"
{ "lsp": { "project_servers": "always" } }
```

`auto` (the default) uses a project's servers when you are watching, `always` uses them every time,
and `never` uses only yours. A project's own config cannot change this.

A language server runs your project's build tooling. rust-analyzer runs `build.rs` and procedural
macros, and a TypeScript server loads `tsconfig.json` plugins. For a repository you do not trust,
use a container rather than relying on this setting.

### Add a language server

```json title="~/.config/luxe/lsp-servers.json"
{
  "ruby": {
    "command": "ruby-lsp",
    "extensions": ["rb"],
    "root_markers": ["Gemfile"],
    "install_hint": "gem install ruby-lsp"
  }
}
```

An entry for a language Luxe already knows changes only what it names, so
`{ "rust": { "command": "rust-analyzer-nightly" } }` swaps the binary and keeps the rest.
`alternatives` lists other servers to try, in order, when the first will not start.

## Debugger

The `debug` tool drives a real debugger, so the agent can set breakpoints, step through code and
inspect variables rather than add print statements. After three failing test runs in a row, Luxe
suggests it. `LUXE_DEBUG_NUDGE=0` turns that suggestion off.

| Language | Adapter |
| --- | --- |
| Python | debugpy (`pip install debugpy`) |
| Rust, C, C++ | CodeLLDB, lldb-dap or gdb |
| Go | Delve (`dlv`) |

`/debug` shows which adapters are installed and any running sessions. To add one, reuse the launch
style of a built-in adapter (`debugpy`, `lldb`, `gdb` or `delve`). This one debugs Zig programs
with `lldb-dap`:

```json title="~/.config/luxe/debug-adapters.json"
[
  {
    "id": "zig",
    "command": ["lldb-dap"],
    "extensions": ["zig"],
    "dialect": "lldb"
  }
]
```

`transport` is `stdio` (the default) or `tcp_dial_in`, for an adapter that connects back to Luxe:
put `${DAP_ADDR}` in its `command` where it takes the address, as Delve's
`dlv dap --client-addr ${DAP_ADDR}` does, and Luxe replaces it with `host:port`.
`addr_placeholder` names a different placeholder.

A breakpoint the adapter could not set is listed under the launch, with the adapter's reason. An
adapter that fails to start says why, with what it printed.

## Web

`web_search` works without a key. To use a particular search provider, set its key; the first one
set is used:

| Key | Provider |
| --- | --- |
| none | Exa, through its public endpoint |
| `BRAVE_API_KEY` | Brave |
| `TAVILY_API_KEY` | Tavily |
| `EXA_API_KEY` | Exa, on your own account |
| `FIRECRAWL_API_KEY` | Firecrawl |

`web_fetch` reads a page as markdown. If a page refuses, it tries again as a browser, and then, with
`FIRECRAWL_API_KEY` set, in a real browser for pages built with JavaScript.

`web_fetch` and `screenshot` reach the internet and your own machine (`localhost`), so your dev
server works. Other machines on your network, cloud metadata addresses and `file://` are refused,
including through an IPv6 address that carries one of them. A page elsewhere can't redirect a fetch
to your machine, and a fetch reads at most 10 MB. `screenshot` loads only the host you asked for, so
a redirect, frame or image from any other host fails to load, and it runs the browser on a fresh
profile, sandboxed unless Luxe runs as root or in a container. `LUXE_WEB_ALLOW_PRIVATE=1` lifts the
address checks, allows `file://` in `screenshot`, and lets it load other hosts. A fetch gives up
after 30 seconds, or `LUXE_WEB_TIMEOUT_SECS`, within the call's 60-second limit.

A search provider's other features, such as crawling a site, are available through its MCP
server; see [MCP](mcp.md).

### GitHub repositories

Given a repository address, such as `https://github.com/owner/repo`, `web_fetch` clones it instead
of reading the page, so the agent can search the real files. The clone is shallow, the latest commit
only, and goes into `.luxe/gh-cache/owner/repo` in your project, which git ignores. Reading it never
asks permission, because it is inside the project.

A repository you did not write sits inside one you did, so Luxe keeps it inert:

- Symbolic links are checked out as plain files holding the link's target. A link cannot point the
  agent at your `.env`, or anywhere else outside the clone.
- Git never prompts. A private repository needs your git credentials for github.com, for example
  from `gh auth setup-git`.
- Git LFS files, submodules and tags are not downloaded.
- Language servers and format-on-save do not start there, because rust-analyzer would run the
  repository's `build.rs`.
- Nothing in it runs unless the agent runs it with `bash`, under your permission rules as usual.

A clone over 500 MB on disk, or one that takes longer than 45 seconds, is stopped and removed.
Fetching a clone more than a day old clones it again, and a clone nobody has fetched in 14 days is
deleted. To clear them all, delete `.luxe/gh-cache/`.

The files are still text the agent reads, and text can carry instructions, so treat a clone like any
other page from the web. To read repositories as web pages instead:

```json title="~/.config/luxe/config.json"
{ "tools": { "clone_repositories": false } }
```
@@@ page: troubleshooting
---
title: "Troubleshooting"
summary: "Common problems, where Luxe logs, and what to include in a bug report."
order: 4
group: "Reference"
---

## Start with `luxe doctor`

```bash
luxe doctor
```

It lists the tools, language servers and debug adapters Luxe found, starts each language server to
check that it works, and shows how to install or fix what does not.

## Common problems

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| **No model selected**, or `--headless` refuses to start | Choose one with `/model`, or pass `--model provider/id`. Luxe never picks one for you. |
| The model picker is empty | No provider is set up. Open **Configuration** (`c`), or set a provider's key in the environment. |
| A provider keeps failing with `retrying (3/3)` | It is overloaded or unreachable. See [When a provider stalls](providers.md#when-a-provider-stalls) for the time limits. |
| A setting does nothing | Luxe ignores keys it does not know, so check the spelling. `luxe init` and `/settings` write a `config.schema.json` your editor can check against. A project's file cannot change some settings; see [Configuration](configuration.md#what-a-project-cannot-change). |
| Icons show as boxes, or sit flush against their words | See [Fonts](install.md#fonts), and the `glyphs` setting in [Appearance](appearance.md#icons-and-fonts). |
| Your terminal's copy key does nothing | The terminal keeps it. Hold `shift` while dragging, or let the key pass through; see [Mouse and clipboard](interface.md#mouse-and-clipboard). |
| Images do not appear | Your terminal may not draw them. `/images` says why; see [Images](appearance.md#images). |
| A language server is not used | `luxe doctor` says whether it starts. A server a project installed is used only when you are watching; see [Tools](tools.md#a-server-the-project-installed). |
| A project's hooks or MCP servers do not run | They need `--trust-project`, or an interactive session for MCP servers. See [Security](security.md#untrusted-repositories). |
| Luxe opened the wrong folder as the project | Inside a repository, a `.luxe/` between you and its top scopes the project there. Remove it, or start Luxe somewhere else. See [Where the project begins](project-context.md#where-the-project-begins). |
| `/pr` or `/github` says GitHub is unavailable | Install the GitHub CLI and sign in: `gh auth login`. A private repository also needs `gh auth setup-git`. |
| A key binding does not work | Your terminal may not send that key. Rebind it; see [Commands and keys](commands.md#rebind-keys). |
| On a Mac, some `alt` keys type a character such as `ø` or `π` | Your terminal treats Option as a key that types characters. Set it to act as Alt; see [Alt keys on a Mac](commands.md#alt-keys-on-a-mac). |

## Logs

A session logs to `.luxe/logs/luxe.log` in the project. Commands that only report, such as
`luxe auth`, `luxe doctor` and `luxe models`, log to `logs/luxe.log` in the state directory:
`~/.local/state/luxe/` (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\luxe\` on Windows), or wherever `LUXE_STATE_DIR` or
`XDG_STATE_HOME` puts it. On macOS and Linux, a log is readable only by you. One past 5 MB is moved
to `luxe.log.1` the next time Luxe starts, replacing the one before.

The log shows Luxe's own activity at `info` and everything else at `warn`. For more:

```bash
LUXE_LOG=debug luxe                        # everything
LUXE_LOG=luxe_core::hooks=debug luxe       # one part, in detail
```

## See what is sent to the model

`LUXE_WIRE_LOG` records every request Luxe sends and every reply, with credentials removed.
`luxe wire` summarizes it: what fills each request, whether the cached part stays the same between
turns, and whether anything is sent twice.

```bash
LUXE_WIRE_LOG=/tmp/wire.jsonl luxe --headless -p "what does src/main.rs do?"
luxe wire /tmp/wire.jsonl
luxe wire /tmp/wire.jsonl --tools    # with each tool's share
```

The log stays on your machine and is off unless the variable is set.

## Report a bug

Open an issue at [github.com/evanwhittaker/luxe](https://github.com/evanwhittaker/luxe/issues) with:

- `luxe --version`, your operating system and terminal
- What you did, what you expected, and what happened
- The relevant part of `.luxe/logs/luxe.log`

If the interface itself draws wrongly, such as stray characters or a half-drawn screen, record the
raw output, which shows what Luxe actually wrote:

```bash
script -f /tmp/luxe.tty -c luxe       # replay with `cat` or `scriptreplay`
asciinema rec /tmp/luxe.cast -c luxe
```

Attach the recording and the log from the same time.
